regiones/iberia/resumen.texto: The peninsula of Spain and Portugal. In the Middle Ages it was at once the Visigothic kingdom, al-Andalus and the Christian kingdoms of the north; the coexistence and clashes of Christians, Muslims and Jews made it the great bridge between Arabic science and Latin Europe.

regiones/iberia/eras.9.nombre.texto: Christian kingdoms and the Nasrid kingdom of Granada

regiones/iberia/eras.0.resumen.texto: The first farmers arrive by the Mediterranean with cardial pottery around 5600 BC; in the west, dolmens are built from the 5th millennium BC.

regiones/iberia/eras.1.resumen.texto: Fortified settlements such as Los Millares and Zambujal and, from around 2700 BC, Bell Beaker. From around 2500 BC people of Steppe ancestry arrive and within a few centuries replace almost all paternal lineages (Olalde et al. 2019).

regiones/iberia/eras.2.resumen.texto: El Argar in the southeast, with settlements on heights and great inequalities in burials; Cogotas I on the Meseta and the Atlantic Bronze Age in the west.

regiones/iberia/eras.3.resumen.texto: The Phoenicians settle at Gadir and along the Andalusian coast; in the lower Guadalquivir Tartessos flourishes, which Herodotus (I.163) associates with King Argantonios, and in the southwest the stelae with the oldest writing in the peninsula are carved.

regiones/iberia/eras.4.resumen.texto: Iberians in the east and south, Celtiberians and other Indo-European peoples in the Meseta and west, Castro culture in the northwest and Greeks at Ampurias; Carthage dominates the south from 237 BC.

regiones/iberia/eras.5.resumen.texto: Rome conquered the Peninsula in two centuries, starting from the Second Punic War; Hispania gave emperors such as Trajan and Hadrian and writers such as Seneca.

regiones/iberia/eras.6.resumen.texto: Vandals, Suebi and Alans entered in 409. The Visigoths ruled the Peninsula from Toledo and converted to Catholicism in 589.

regiones/iberia/eras.7.resumen.texto: Al-Andalus occupied almost the whole Peninsula and Córdoba was the largest city in the West; in the north Asturias, León, Navarre and the Catalan counties arose.

regiones/iberia/eras.8.resumen.texto: Al-Andalus split into taifa kingdoms, which two Berber empires reunified; Castile, Aragon and Portugal advanced to the Guadalquivir.

regiones/iberia/eras.9.resumen.texto: Castile, Aragon, Portugal and Navarre dominated the Peninsula; only the Muslim kingdom of Granada remained, conquered in 1492.

regiones/iberia/eras.10.resumen.texto: The Iberian kingdoms turned to their overseas empires; Spain and Portugal were united between 1580 and 1640.

regiones/iberia/eras.11.resumen.texto: Napoleonic wars, the independence of America, liberal revolutions and, in the 20th century, dictatorships and democracies.

regiones/iberia/demografia.0.nota.texto: Sum of Spain, Portugal, Andorra and Gibraltar within their present borders (including the Balearic and Canary Islands, the Azores and Madeira).

regiones/iberia/demografia.15.nota.texto: Urlanis (1941) gives 9 million for the year 1000.

regiones/iberia/demografia.16.nota.texto: Urlanis (1941) gives 6 million for 1300 and 5 for 1350: the two series differ greatly.

regiones/iberia/religiones.1.nombre.texto: Religions of the Celtic and other Indo-European peoples

regiones/iberia/religiones.0.nota.texto: The temple of Melqart (the Greeks' Heracles) at Gadir was famous across the Mediterranean.

regiones/iberia/religiones.1.nota.texto: The majority religion by extent. We know it almost only from Latin inscriptions to native gods (Endovellicus, Ataecina, Bandua, Nabia, Lugus) and from Strabo (III.3.7), who tells of sacrifices of he-goats, prisoners and horses to a god of war among the mountain peoples of the north.

regiones/iberia/religiones.3.nota.texto: Sanctuaries with thousands of bronze ex-votos (Collado de los Jardines, El Castellar) and stone ones (Cerro de los Santos); the Iberian texts are not understood.

regiones/iberia/religiones.6.nota.texto: Expelled from Castile and Aragon in 1492 and from Portugal in 1497.

regiones/iberia/religiones.8.nota.texto: The Suebi converted to Catholicism around 560 and the Visigoths in 589.

regiones/iberia/religiones.10.nota.texto: According to the estimate of Bulliet (1979), based on the names of Andalusi biographers, most of the population of al-Andalus had converted by the 10th century. In the Christian north there was no conversion.

regiones/iberia/religiones.14.nota.texto: Forcibly baptized between 1500 and 1526 and expelled between 1609 and 1614.

regiones/iberia/culturas.3.nombre.texto: Bronze Age (El Argar, Cogotas I, Atlantic Bronze Age)

regiones/iberia/culturas.7.nombre.texto: Celts of the Meseta and the west (Celtiberians, Vaccaei, Vettones, Carpetani, Celtici)

regiones/iberia/culturas.0.nota.texto: Farmers who descended mostly from those of Anatolia, mixed with local hunter-gatherers (Haak et al. 2015).

regiones/iberia/culturas.2.nota.texto: The peninsula is one of the oldest centers of Bell Beaker; unlike Britain, here Steppe ancestry does not arrive with it but somewhat later (Olalde et al. 2018 and 2019).

regiones/iberia/culturas.4.nota.texto: Gadir (Cádiz), Malaka, Sexi and Abdera. Tradition puts the founding of Gadir in 1104 BC; archaeology, in the 9th or 8th century BC. Carthage dominates the south between 237 and 206 BC.

regiones/iberia/culturas.5.nota.texto: Tartessos appears in Herodotus (I.163, IV.152) and in the Orientalizing archaeology of the lower Guadalquivir (El Carambolo); afterwards the area belongs to the Turdetani, whom Strabo (III.1.6) describes as the most cultured people of Iberia, with laws in verse.

regiones/iberia/culturas.6.nota.texto: Whether they were Celts is debated people by people. In the northwest there are many Celtic names (the -briga names, the Celtici of Pliny) alongside others from a non-Celtic Indo-European language (Prósper 2002); of the Astures and Cantabrians mostly personal and place names remain, Indo-European and partly Celtic. Many archaeologists also stress the local development of the castros from the Late Bronze Age (González-Ruibal 2007). Castro culture in the strict sense is that of the northwest; the Cantabrians also lived in castros, with features of their own.

regiones/iberia/culturas.7.nota.texto: Largest by extent: Indo-European-speaking peoples occupied the Meseta and the west, more than half the peninsula (the area of the -briga toponyms mapped by Untermann); the east and south, more populous, were Iberian and Turdetanian. Herodotus (II.33) already places Celts beyond the Pillars of Heracles; how much of this was “Celtic” and when it arrived is debated.

regiones/iberia/culturas.8.nota.texto: Emporion, founded by Phocaeans from Massalia around 575 BC, and Rhode (Roses).

regiones/iberia/culturas.9.nota.texto: Peoples speaking non-Indo-European languages, from eastern Andalusia to the Roussillon (Contestani, Edetani, Ilergetes, Layetani and others), with their sanctuaries, their stone ladies (Elche, Baza) and their writing.

regiones/iberia/culturas.10.nota.texto: Grows with the conquest and colonies, such as Italica (206 BC) and Carteia (171 BC).

regiones/iberia/culturas.11.nota.texto: The Lusitanians appear in the sources at the beginning of the 2nd century BC (Livy XXXV.1) and resisted Rome under Viriathus (147-139 BC); whether their language was Celtic is debated.

regiones/iberia/culturas.12.nota.texto: The Vascones appear in Roman sources during the Sertorian war (76 BC); their language predates the arrival of the Indo-Europeans.

regiones/iberia/idiomas.0.nota.texto: Nobody knows what languages the Neolithic farmers spoke: they left no texts. They are assumed to predate the Indo-European ones because genetics shows that these arrived later, with people of Steppe ancestry; their traces are sought in place names and loanwords, with much-disputed theories.

regiones/iberia/idiomas.1.nota.texto: The ancestors of Iberian and Basque, which survived in the east, the south and the north.

regiones/iberia/idiomas.2.nota.texto: Genetics shows the arrival of people of Steppe ancestry from around 2500 BC (Olalde et al. 2019), and the western half of the peninsula speaks Indo-European languages when it appears in the texts; when the Celtic languages arrived is debated.

regiones/iberia/idiomas.4.nota.texto: About 95 stelae from southern Portugal and western Andalusia, in a script derived from Phoenician; they are usually dated to the 7th century BC, with proposals between the 8th and the 5th. Koch (Tartessian, 2009, and later works) reads it as Celtic; most specialists leave it unclassified.

regiones/iberia/idiomas.6.nota.texto: Non-Indo-European language written from the 5th century BC to the turn of the era, with its own sign systems and with the Greek alphabet; the signs have been read since Gómez-Moreno, but the texts are not understood. Whether it is related to Basque is debated.

regiones/iberia/idiomas.7.nota.texto: Majority by extent, in the Meseta and the west. We know them by names since Herodotus (II.33, around 450 BC), who places Celts beyond the Pillars of Heracles, and by inscriptions since the 2nd century BC; they are certainly earlier. The count includes the northwest, whose language we know only from names, largely Celtic, and sets aside Lusitanian.

regiones/iberia/idiomas.9.nota.texto: A handful of inscriptions from the 1st and 2nd centuries in Latin letters (Cabeço das Fráguas, Lamas de Moledo, Arroyo de la Luz). It is Indo-European; whether it is Celtic is debated: it keeps the Indo-European p (porcom, “pig”, in Cabeço das Fráguas), which Celtic lost, and so most scholars set it apart (Untermann, Gorrochategui); a minority considers it Celtic or very close to it.

regiones/iberia/idiomas.10.nota.texto: The Vascones appear in Roman sources during the Sertorian war (76 BC); their language predates the arrival of the Indo-Europeans.

regiones/iberia/idiomas.16.nota.texto: In al-Andalus it coexisted with Andalusi Romance: many people were bilingual.

regiones/francia/resumen.texto: Ancient Gaul, kingdom of the Franks and later of France. It was the center of the reformed monasticism of Cluny and the Cistercians, of Gothic art, of the Crusades and, with the schools and University of Paris, of scholastic thought.

regiones/francia/eras.0.resumen.texto: The first farmers arrive by the Mediterranean (impressed and cardial pottery, around 5800 BC) and by the Danube (band pottery, around 5000 BC); in Brittany some of the oldest megaliths in Europe are raised.

regiones/francia/eras.1.resumen.texto: Bell Beaker vessels spread across all of France; with them arrive people of Steppe ancestry (Brunel et al. 2020).

regiones/francia/eras.2.resumen.texto: Atlantic Bronze Age in the west, with axes and swords circulating from Iberia to Ireland, and from around 1300 BC the Urnfield culture in the east.

regiones/francia/eras.3.resumen.texto: Princely residences in the east, such as Mont Lassois, with the Vix burial (around 500 BC) and its Greek krater; the Phocaeans found Massalia around 600 BC.

regiones/francia/eras.4.resumen.texto: La Tène art, Gaulish migrations to Italy and the Danube (4th century BC), and from the 2nd century BC oppida and coinage. Rome conquers the south (Narbonensis, 121 BC) and Caesar the rest (58-50 BC).

regiones/francia/eras.5.resumen.texto: Conquered by Caesar, Gaul was Romanized and Christianized; in the 5th century it was occupied by Visigoths, Burgundians and Franks.

regiones/francia/eras.6.resumen.texto: Clovis and his descendants united Gaul under the Franks, with frequent divisions among heirs.

regiones/francia/eras.7.resumen.texto: The Carolingians built an empire under Charlemagne; from the Treaty of Verdun (843) the west became the kingdom of West Francia.

regiones/francia/eras.8.resumen.texto: The Capetian kings expanded their domain against the great lords and the kings of England; Paris was the intellectual center of Europe.

regiones/francia/eras.9.resumen.texto: The Valois disputed the throne with the kings of England; war, plague and revolts devastated the kingdom.

regiones/francia/eras.10.resumen.texto: The kings of France unified the territory and built an absolute monarchy.

regiones/francia/eras.11.resumen.texto: Revolution, the Napoleonic empire, republics and the two world wars.

regiones/francia/demografia.0.nota.texto: France (including Corsica, excluding the overseas territories, which the UN counts separately) and Monaco, within their present borders.

regiones/francia/demografia.10.nota.texto: This is not the population: Plutarch says Caesar fought against three million men, killed a million and took as many prisoners; Appian gives similar figures and Pliny (Natural History VII.92) counts 1,192,000 dead in his battles. These are round numbers that come from what Caesar and his panegyrists spread, with no way to check them; Henige (“He came, he saw, we counted”, 1998) shows that they cannot be used as data. That they are inflated does not mean the war was not devastating: Caesar himself says he sold 53,000 Aduatuci into slavery (Commentaries on the Gallic War II.33) and the surviving Veneti (III.16). What cannot be measured is how much Gaul was depopulated.

regiones/francia/demografia.11.nota.texto: Gaul and Germania: the Three Gauls, Narbonensis and the two Germanies (about 635,000 km²); includes Belgium, Switzerland and the left bank of the Rhine, which this region does not have.

regiones/francia/demografia.12.nota.texto: Gaul and Germania: the Three Gauls, Narbonensis and the two Germanies (about 680,000 km²); includes Belgium, Switzerland and the left bank of the Rhine, which this region does not have. Mid-2nd century.

regiones/francia/demografia.13.nota.texto: Gaul and Germania: the Three Gauls, Narbonensis and the two Germanies (about 635,000 km²); includes Belgium, Switzerland and the left bank of the Rhine, which this region does not have.

regiones/francia/demografia.14.nota.texto: France and the Low Countries together.

regiones/francia/demografia.15.nota.texto: France and the Low Countries together.

regiones/francia/demografia.16.nota.texto: France and the Low Countries together. Urlanis (1941) gives 9 million for France alone.

regiones/francia/demografia.17.nota.texto: France and the Low Countries together. For France alone, Urlanis (1941) gives 17 million in 1300 and 15 in 1350.

regiones/francia/demografia.18.nota.texto: France and the Low Countries together.

regiones/francia/religiones.1.nota.texto: We know it from Greek and Roman authors (Caesar, Gallic War VI.13-18; Posidonius through Diodorus and Strabo; Lucan), from sanctuaries such as Gournay-sur-Aronde and Ribemont-sur-Ancre (4th to 1st century BC) and from dedications of the Roman period; the Gauls left almost nothing written about it.

regiones/francia/religiones.5.nota.texto: Expelled from the kingdom in 1306 and, after their return, in 1394; they remained in Provence and Avignon.

regiones/francia/culturas.0.nota.texto: Farmers who arrived by the Mediterranean and by the Danube, descending mostly from those of Anatolia mixed with local hunter-gatherers (Brunel et al. 2020).

regiones/francia/culturas.1.nota.texto: Bell Beaker vessels in individual graves; in France they coincide with the arrival of Steppe ancestry (Brunel et al. 2020). Whether it was a people, a fashion or an exchange network is debated.

regiones/francia/culturas.5.nota.texto: The Early Iron Age culture of eastern France; the west and south have their own groups. It is usually linked to the ancestors of the Gauls, but that they spoke Celtic is inferred, not documented.

regiones/francia/culturas.6.nota.texto: Massalia (Marseille), founded by Phocaeans around 600 BC, and its coastal colonies, such as Agde, Antibes and Nice; it lost its independence to Caesar in 49 BC.

regiones/francia/culturas.7.nota.texto: The Greeks called the peoples of Provence Ligurians; Strabo (IV.6.3) calls the Salluvii, defeated by Rome in 123-122 BC, “celtoligures”.

regiones/francia/culturas.8.nota.texto: Graffiti in Iberian script at Ensérune and Pech Maho, from the 5th century BC.

regiones/francia/culturas.9.nota.texto: The Greeks have called the peoples of the interior beyond Massalia keltoi since Hecataeus (around 500 BC); Caesar (Gallic War I.1) divides Gaul into Belgae, Aquitani and Celts, “who in our language are called Gauls”. Collis (The Celts: Origins, Myths and Inventions, 2003) disputes that “Celt” names a people and not a Greek label.

regiones/francia/culturas.11.nota.texto: The Aquitani, between the Garonne and the Pyrenees, appear in Caesar (56 BC); the names of people and gods in their Latin inscriptions show a language related to the ancestor of Basque (Mitxelena, Gorrochategui).

regiones/francia/culturas.16.nota.texto: In the French Basque Country (Labourd, Lower Navarre and Soule).

regiones/francia/idiomas.0.nota.texto: Nobody knows what languages the Neolithic farmers spoke: they left no texts. They are assumed to predate the Indo-European ones because genetics shows that these arrived later, with people of Steppe ancestry; their traces are sought in place names and loanwords, with much-disputed theories.

regiones/francia/idiomas.1.nota.texto: No texts. That they were Indo-European is inferred from the arrival of people of Steppe ancestry (Haak et al. 2015; Olalde et al. 2018) and from the fact that the first documented languages of the area are Indo-European; when and where Proto-Celtic arose is debated (Koch and Cunliffe: the Atlantic in the Bronze Age; Sims-Williams 2020: Bronze Age Gaul, between the centre and the west of Europe).

regiones/francia/idiomas.2.nota.texto: Varro, quoted by Isidore of Seville (Etymologies, book XV), called the Massaliots trilingual because they spoke Greek, Latin and Gaulish.

regiones/francia/idiomas.3.nota.texto: Poorly known language, known from place names and personal names; whether it was Indo-European is debated.

regiones/francia/idiomas.5.nota.texto: Before the first Gallo-Greek inscriptions (3rd century BC) it is shown by the names of people, peoples and places transmitted by Greeks and Romans; Lepontic, very close, was already written in the 6th century BC.

regiones/francia/idiomas.7.nota.texto: The Aquitani appear in Caesar (56 BC); their personal and divine names in Latin inscriptions show a language related to the ancestor of Basque (Mitxelena, Gorrochategui).

regiones/francia/idiomas.9.nota.texto: It continued to be spoken during the Empire: shown by the potters' accounts of La Graufesenque (1st century), the Larzac tablet and the Chamalières lead.

regiones/francia/idiomas.10.nota.texto: The last testimonies are debated: Jerome compares the language of the Treveri with that of the Galatians (around 387), Sulpicius Severus has a character speak “in Celtic or, if you prefer, in Gaulish” (around 400) and Gregory of Tours names a temple called Vasso Galatae “in the Gaulish language” (6th century).

regiones/francia/idiomas.13.nota.texto: In the French Basque Country; it continues the language of the Aquitani.

regiones/britania/resumen.texto: England, Wales and Scotland. After the end of Roman rule came the Anglo-Saxons, then the Vikings and, in 1066, the Normans; the monasteries of Northumbria produced Bede and Alcuin, and Oxford the logic and natural philosophy of Grosseteste, Bacon, Scotus and Ockham.

regiones/britania/eras.7.nombre.texto: Vikings and the kingdom of England

regiones/britania/eras.0.resumen.texto: Hunter-gatherers on an island already separated from the continent by the sea. Their last groups are replaced by the farmers who arrive around 4000 BC.

regiones/britania/eras.1.resumen.texto: The first farmers arrive from the continent around 4000 BC and almost completely replace the hunters (Brace et al. 2019); they build long barrows and, from around 3000 BC, Stonehenge.

regiones/britania/eras.2.resumen.texto: With the Beaker culture comes a people of Steppe ancestry who within a few centuries replace around 90% of the island's gene pool (Olalde et al. 2018). Around 1000–875 BC another wave arrives from France, which Patterson et al. (2022) propose as the route by which Celtic languages entered Britain.

regiones/britania/eras.3.resumen.texto: Hillforts such as Maiden Castle and Danebury, brochs in the north and the Arras culture in Yorkshire. Pytheas travels around the island around 325 BC, and Caesar invades in 55 and 54 BC.

regiones/britania/eras.4.resumen.texto: The island was a Roman province up to Hadrian's Wall, and at times up to the Antonine Wall; Rome abandoned it around 410.

regiones/britania/eras.5.resumen.texto: Angles, Saxons and Jutes settled in the east. Gildas and Bede tell it as a conquest that drove out the Britons; genetics shows a large migration from northern Germany, the Netherlands and Denmark that mixed with the local population (Gretzinger et al., 2022).

regiones/britania/eras.6.resumen.texto: Northumbria, Mercia, Wessex and other kingdoms converted to Christianity; monasteries flourished.

regiones/britania/eras.7.resumen.texto: The Danes conquered the north and east; Wessex resisted and unified England in the 10th century.

regiones/britania/eras.8.resumen.texto: The Normans imposed a new nobility; the Plantagenets also ruled half of France until the Hundred Years' War.

regiones/britania/eras.9.resumen.texto: Anglican Reformation, union of the crowns of England and Scotland (1603), and the revolutions of the 17th century.

regiones/britania/eras.10.resumen.texto: Union with Scotland, the British Empire and the Industrial Revolution.

regiones/britania/demografia.0.nota.texto: United Kingdom (including Northern Ireland), the Isle of Man and the Channel Islands, within their present borders.

regiones/britania/demografia.11.nota.texto: Roman Britain (about 160,000 km²), without northern Scotland; mid-2nd century.

regiones/britania/demografia.13.nota.texto: Late 4th century: about 125,000 were soldiers with their families and about 240,000 lived in towns. This is considerably more than what Harper (2017) proposes for the 2nd century.

regiones/britania/demografia.14.nota.texto: Sum of England and Wales (1.6) and Scotland (0.3).

regiones/britania/demografia.18.nota.texto: England and Wales and Scotland. Other authors give between 3.7 and 7 million for England alone before the plague.

regiones/britania/religiones.7.nombre.texto: Church of England and Scottish Presbyterianism

regiones/britania/religiones.0.nota.texto: No texts of their own: deposits in rivers and lakes (the Battersea shield, Llyn Cerrig Bach) and what Caesar (Gallic War VI.13: druidism “originated in Britain”) and Tacitus (Annals XIV.30, the island of Mona) say. Calling it Celtic from 800 BC is an inference.

regiones/britania/religiones.6.nota.texto: Jews arrived with the Normans and were expelled in 1290.

regiones/britania/culturas.0.nota.texto: Hunter-gatherers; no writing, so what is known comes from archaeology and ancient DNA (Brace et al. 2019).

regiones/britania/culturas.1.nota.texto: Farmers who descended mostly from people of Anatolia, mixed with the local hunters (Haak et al. 2015).

regiones/britania/culturas.2.nota.texto: In Britain the Beaker period coincides with a great population replacement (Olalde et al. 2018).

regiones/britania/culturas.5.nota.texto: That they spoke Celtic languages is shown by the names transmitted by Caesar, Tacitus and Ptolemy; but no ancient author called the Britons “Celts”, and James (The Atlantic Celts, 1999) and Collis question using that word for them.

regiones/britania/idiomas.0.nota.texto: No one knows what languages the Mesolithic hunters spoke: they left no texts. They are assumed to predate the Indo-European languages, which, according to the steppe hypothesis, arrived later with people of Steppe ancestry.

regiones/britania/idiomas.1.nota.texto: No one knows what languages the Neolithic farmers spoke: they left no texts. They are assumed to predate the Indo-European languages, because genetics shows that these arrived later, with people of Steppe ancestry. Traces are sought in place names and loanwords, with much-disputed theories.

regiones/britania/idiomas.2.nota.texto: No texts. That they were Indo-European is inferred from the arrival of people of Steppe ancestry (Haak et al. 2015; Olalde et al. 2018) and from the fact that the first documented languages of the area are Indo-European. When and where Proto-Celtic arose is disputed (Koch and Cunliffe: the Atlantic in the Bronze Age; Sims-Williams 2020: Bronze Age Gaul, between central and western Europe). Patterson et al. (2022) link the arrival of Celtic in Britain to the migration from France around 1000–875 BC.

regiones/britania/idiomas.3.nota.texto: The first evidence consists of names: Pytheas's “Pretanic” islands (around 325 BC), coin legends (from the 1st century BC), and the names given by Caesar, Tacitus and Ptolemy.

regiones/britania/idiomas.6.nota.texto: Today most scholars consider it a Brittonic language (Forsyth, Language in Pictland, 1997).

regiones/irlanda/resumen.texto: The island that was never Roman. Christianized in the 5th century, its monasteries preserved Latin and Greek, copied books such as the Book of Kells and sent missionaries and teachers to the continent, such as Columbanus and John Scotus Eriugena.

regiones/irlanda/eras.0.resumen.texto: Late Mesolithic: hunter-gatherers and fishers with a large-flake industry (of the Bann type), in camps such as Ferriter's Cove (southwest) and Newferry (north), until the arrival of the first farmers. Older sites, such as Mount Sandel (around 7000 BC), Lough Boora and the Hermitage burial (7530–7320 BC), predate this era.

regiones/irlanda/eras.1.resumen.texto: The first farmers arrive around 3750 BC (Cassidy et al. 2016); they build the enclosed fields of Céide and passage tombs such as Newgrange (around 3200 BC).

regiones/irlanda/eras.2.resumen.texto: Beaker culture and the copper mines of Ross Island; with them comes Steppe ancestry (Cassidy et al. 2016). In the Late Bronze Age there is a great deal of gold metalwork.

regiones/irlanda/eras.3.resumen.texto: Gaelic kingdoms without cities or writing, apart from the Ogham inscriptions.

regiones/irlanda/eras.4.resumen.texto: After Patrick's mission, great monasteries such as Clonmacnoise and Armagh became centers of learning and mission.

regiones/irlanda/eras.5.resumen.texto: The Vikings founded Dublin and other cities; the Gaelic kings contested the title of high king.

regiones/irlanda/eras.6.resumen.texto: The Anglo-Normans conquered part of the island for the king of England, although Gaelic lords recovered much of the territory.

regiones/irlanda/eras.7.resumen.texto: Tudor conquest, Protestant colonization, union with Great Britain (1801) and the Great Famine (1845–1849).

regiones/irlanda/eras.8.resumen.texto: The Irish Free State and then the republic; the north remained in the United Kingdom.

regiones/irlanda/demografia.9.nota.texto: Republic of Ireland; Northern Ireland is counted under Britain.

regiones/irlanda/religiones.0.nota.texto: Since the Celtic Iron Age (c. 500 BC); there is no earlier record.

regiones/irlanda/culturas.0.nota.texto: Hunter-gatherers; no writing, so what is known comes from archaeology and ancient DNA.

regiones/irlanda/culturas.1.nota.texto: Farmers who descended mostly from people of Anatolia, mixed with the local hunters (Haak et al. 2015).

regiones/irlanda/culturas.5.nota.texto: From the Celtic Iron Age (around 500 BC) onward; there is no record before that.

They are assumed to predate the Indo-European languages, because genetics shows that these arrived later, with people of Steppe ancestry. Traces are sought in place names and loanwords, with much-disputed theories.

regiones/irlanda/idiomas.2.nota.texto: No texts. When and where Proto-Celtic arose is disputed (Koch and Cunliffe: the Atlantic in the Bronze Age; Sims-Williams 2020: Bronze Age Gaul, between central and western Europe). For Ireland, Mallory (The Origins of the Irish, 2013) reviews the hypotheses about the arrival of Goidelic.

regiones/irlanda/idiomas.3.nota.texto: From the Celtic Iron Age (around 500 BC) onward; it has been written since the 4th century, in Ogham.

regiones/alemania/resumen.texto: The German- and Dutch-speaking lands: present-day Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Switzerland and Austria, the core of the Holy Roman Empire. It was a land of Carolingian missions, of the monasteries of Fulda and Reichenau, of the Hanseatic cities, of Rhineland mysticism and of the printing press.

regiones/alemania/eras.7.nombre.texto: Holy Roman Empire of the Ottonians, Salians and Staufen

regiones/alemania/eras.8.nombre.texto: Empire of the princes and cities

regiones/alemania/eras.9.nombre.texto: Reformation and the early modern Holy Roman Empire

regiones/alemania/eras.0.resumen.texto: The Linear Pottery culture brings agriculture from Hungary to the Rhine around 5500-5000 BC; from around 2900 BC, Corded Ware brings people of Steppe ancestry (Haak et al. 2015).

regiones/alemania/eras.1.resumen.texto: Únětice, barrows and urnfields in the centre and south; Nordic Bronze Age in the north. The Nebra sky disc was buried around 1600 BC.

regiones/alemania/eras.2.resumen.texto: Princely residences in the southwest (Heuneburg, Hochdorf, Glauberg) and the Hallstatt salt mine, which gives the period its name; in the north, the Jastorf culture from the 6th century BC.

regiones/alemania/eras.3.resumen.texto: In the south and centre, Celts with oppida such as Manching and La Tène art, whose type site is on Lake Neuchâtel; in the north, Germanic peoples. Caesar reaches the Rhine (58-51 BC) and Augustus conquers the Alps and the Danube (15 BC).

regiones/alemania/eras.4.resumen.texto: Rome dominated the Rhine and the Danube; to the east lived Germanic peoples who pressed on it until they crossed the frontier in the 5th century.

regiones/alemania/eras.5.resumen.texto: The Franks subjected the Alemanni, Thuringians, Bavarians and, under Charlemagne, the Saxons; missionaries such as Boniface founded bishoprics and monasteries.

regiones/alemania/eras.6.resumen.texto: The Treaty of Verdun gave rise to the kingdom of East Francia; the Saxon kings held back the Hungarians.

regiones/alemania/eras.7.resumen.texto: The kings of Germany were emperors, clashed with the papacy and expanded eastward.

regiones/alemania/eras.8.resumen.texto: Power passed to the electoral and territorial princes and to the free cities; the Hanseatic League flourished.

regiones/alemania/eras.9.resumen.texto: Luther, wars of religion, the Thirty Years' War and the rise of Austria and Prussia.

regiones/alemania/eras.10.resumen.texto: Germany, Austria, Switzerland, the Netherlands, Belgium and Luxembourg as separate states.

regiones/alemania/demografia.0.nota.texto: Sum of Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Belgium, Switzerland, Luxembourg and Liechtenstein within their present borders.

regiones/alemania/demografia.10.nota.texto: According to tablets with Greek letters found in the Helvetian camp: 263,000 Helvetii, 36,000 Tulingi, 14,000 Latobrigi, 23,000 Rauraci and 32,000 Boii, of whom 92,000 could bear arms; after the defeat 110,000 returned. It is a single migrating group, not the population of the region. That the lists were in Greek letters is plausible: the Gauls wrote their language in that alphabet (Caesar himself says so in VI.14, and the Gallo-Greek inscriptions show it). The figures, however, are Caesar's, who had an interest in enlarging his victory, and cannot be verified: Henige (1998) considers them implausible (it strikes him that the armed men are exactly a quarter) and many historians reduce them greatly; that the migration was large no one disputes.

regiones/alemania/demografia.21.nota.texto: Sum of Urlanis's figures for Germany within the 1914 borders, Switzerland, Belgium and the Netherlands. Germany of 1914 includes territories now in Poland and does not include Austria.

regiones/alemania/demografia.22.nota.texto: Germany (1914), Switzerland, Belgium and the Netherlands.

regiones/alemania/demografia.29.nota.texto: Germany (1914), Switzerland, Belgium and the Netherlands.

regiones/alemania/religiones.4.nombre.texto: Celtic cults in the Roman period (Matronae, Sirona, Apollo Grannus)

regiones/alemania/religiones.1.nota.texto: No texts from the period: sanctuaries and votive deposits, and what Roman authors later say.

regiones/alemania/religiones.2.nota.texto: The Saxons were forcibly baptized in Charlemagne's wars (772-804).

regiones/alemania/religiones.4.nota.texto: Hundreds of altars to the Matronae in the Rhineland, of Celtic and Germanic cult, and dedications to Celtic gods identified with Roman ones, such as Apollo Grannus.

regiones/alemania/religiones.8.nota.texto: From the 16th century, northern Germany and the Netherlands were mostly Protestant, and the south, Austria and Belgium Catholic.

regiones/alemania/culturas.8.nombre.texto: La Tène Celtic (Helvetii, Vindelici, Treveri, Belgae and others)

regiones/alemania/culturas.0.nota.texto: Farmers who descended mostly from those of Anatolia, mixed with local hunter-gatherers (Haak et al. 2015).

regiones/alemania/culturas.1.nota.texto: With it arrives people of Steppe ancestry (Haak et al. 2015); many link it with the spread of the Indo-European languages.

regiones/alemania/culturas.7.nota.texto: From the Jastorf culture, the first associated with Germanic peoples.

regiones/alemania/culturas.8.nota.texto: In the south and centre, up to the middle mountains of Germany; in the north lived Germanic peoples. How much they mixed in the strip between the two is debated: Caesar (II.4) says that most of the Belgae came from the Germans, but the leaders of the “Germans” of northern Gaul, such as Ambiorix, have Celtic names.

regiones/alemania/culturas.9.nota.texto: From the Jastorf culture (around 500 BC), the first associated with Germanic peoples.

regiones/alemania/culturas.10.nota.texto: A large part of the population of the Rhine and Danube provinces was Celtic.

regiones/alemania/idiomas.2.nota.texto: From the Jastorf culture; until the first centuries AD it is common Germanic.

regiones/alemania/idiomas.3.nota.texto: Non-Indo-European language related to Etruscan, written in alphabets of northern Italy between the 5th and 1st centuries BC.

regiones/alemania/idiomas.4.nota.texto: We know them from names of people, peoples and places, from coin legends and, already in the Roman period, from inscriptions: the Gaulish of the Helvetii and the Treveri and the Noric of the east.

regiones/alemania/idiomas.5.nota.texto: From the Jastorf culture (around 500 BC); until the first centuries AD it is common Germanic, still undivided.

regiones/alemania/idiomas.6.nota.texto: Jerome (around 387) says that the Treveri spoke almost the same language as the Galatians of Asia.

regiones/escandinavia/resumen.texto: Denmark, Norway and Sweden, the land of the Vikings. Its seafarers raided and traded from Ireland to Byzantium and reached Iceland, Greenland and America; between the 10th and 12th centuries they became Christian kingdoms.

regiones/escandinavia/eras.0.resumen.texto: Chiefdoms and small kingdoms, with major cult centers such as Uppsala and trade in the Baltic.

regiones/escandinavia/eras.1.resumen.texto: Norse raids, trade and settlements from the Atlantic to the Volga; the kingdoms of Denmark, Norway and Sweden emerged.

regiones/escandinavia/eras.2.resumen.texto: Archbishoprics in Lund, Nidaros and Uppsala, written laws and competition with the Hanseatic League.

regiones/escandinavia/eras.3.resumen.texto: The three kingdoms shared a king until Sweden broke away under Gustav Vasa.

regiones/escandinavia/eras.4.resumen.texto: Lutheran Reformation and the rivalry of two powers over the Baltic.

regiones/escandinavia/eras.5.resumen.texto: Norway separated from Denmark and later from Sweden (1905); the three kingdoms built welfare states.

regiones/escandinavia/demografia.0.nota.texto: Sum of Sweden, Norway, Denmark, the Faroe Islands and Svalbard within their present borders.

regiones/escandinavia/demografia.20.nota.texto: Sum of Denmark, Sweden and Norway.

regiones/escandinavia/religiones.0.nota.texto: Since the Pre-Roman Iron Age (c. 500 BC); before that, the Nordic Bronze Age.

regiones/escandinavia/religiones.1.nota.texto: Denmark was Christianized under Harald Bluetooth c. 965, Norway under the two Olafs (995–1030) and Sweden later: the temple at Uppsala was still active c. 1075.

regiones/escandinavia/culturas.1.nombre.texto: German merchants of the Hanseatic League

regiones/escandinavia/culturas.0.nota.texto: Since the Pre-Roman Iron Age (c. 500 BC); before that, the Nordic Bronze Age.

regiones/escandinavia/idiomas.0.nombre.texto: Old Norse, later Danish, Swedish and Norwegian

regiones/escandinavia/idiomas.0.nota.texto: Since the Pre-Roman Iron Age (c. 500 BC); written in runes from the 2nd century.

regiones/escandinavia/idiomas.1.nota.texto: First certain mention c. 550: Procopius's skrithiphinoi and Jordanes's screrefennae, hunters who traveled on skis.

regiones/islandia/resumen.texto: North Atlantic island settled by Norwegians and their Gaelic slaves from 870. Without a king until 1262, it governed itself through its assembly, the Althing, and produced the richest medieval literature of the North: the Eddas and the sagas.

regiones/islandia/eras.0.resumen.texto: Until the Norse settlement of 870 the island had no permanent population. Papar is the term with which Ari the Learned (Íslendingabók, 12th century) calls the Irish hermits; Dicuil recounts that clerics spent time in Thule around 795. These testimonies and the finds prior to 870 are disputed.

regiones/islandia/eras.1.resumen.texto: Norwegian settlers and settlers from the British Isles occupied the coasts; the Book of Settlements records their families.

regiones/islandia/eras.2.resumen.texto: A state without a king, with a general assembly and courts; in the 13th century wars between great families opened the way to the king of Norway.

regiones/islandia/eras.3.resumen.texto: The Icelanders swore allegiance to the king of Norway; it was the age in which the great sagas were written.

regiones/islandia/eras.4.resumen.texto: The island passed with Norway to the Danish crown; the Reformation was imposed in 1550.

regiones/islandia/eras.5.resumen.texto: Sovereign kingdom in personal union with Denmark from 1918 and a republic from 1944.

regiones/islandia/demografia.0.nota.texto: Iceland. It was uninhabited until the arrival of the Norse, c. 874: earlier values from the HYDE model are not shown.

regiones/islandia/demografia.8.nota.texto: The first complete census of a country: it recorded 50,358 people, after several epidemics and famines.

regiones/islandia/culturas.1.nota.texto: Genetic studies indicate that a large share of the island's first women came from Ireland and Scotland.

regiones/polonia/resumen.texto: The lands of the Piasts between the Oder and the Bug. Christianized in the Latin rite in 966, Poland resisted the Mongols and the Teutonic Order and, united with Lithuania from 1386, was one of the largest powers of Eastern Europe.

regiones/polonia/eras.2.nombre.texto: Iron Age: Celts, Przeworsk and Wielbark

regiones/polonia/eras.0.resumen.texto: Band pottery in Silesia and Kuyavia from around 5400 BC; then funnel-necked beakers, globular amphorae and, from around 2800 BC, Corded Ware.

regiones/polonia/eras.1.resumen.texto: Únětice and barrows; from around 1300 BC, the Lusatian culture, of urnfields, with fortified settlements such as Biskupin (8th century BC).

regiones/polonia/eras.2.resumen.texto: Celts in Silesia and Lesser Poland (4th to 1st centuries BC); then the Przeworsk and Wielbark cultures, which are usually identified with Vandals and Goths.

regiones/polonia/eras.3.resumen.texto: Polans, Vistulans, Masovians and other Slavic peoples with fortified centers.

regiones/polonia/eras.4.resumen.texto: Mieszko I and Bolesław the Brave created a Christian state with an archbishopric at Gniezno.

regiones/polonia/eras.5.resumen.texto: The kingdom was divided among the sons of Bolesław III; German colonists arrived, and then came the Mongol invasion of 1241.

regiones/polonia/eras.6.resumen.texto: Władysław the Short and Casimir the Great reunited the kingdom, codified its laws and founded the University of Kraków.

regiones/polonia/eras.7.resumen.texto: Union with Lithuania, victory over the Teutonic Order and the flowering of the Renaissance in Kraków.

regiones/polonia/eras.8.resumen.texto: An elective monarchy with a powerful nobility, until the partitions among Russia, Prussia and Austria.

regiones/polonia/eras.9.resumen.texto: Without a state of its own, with uprisings against Russia in 1830 and 1863.

regiones/polonia/eras.10.resumen.texto: Independence, Nazi and Soviet occupation, the Holocaust, a communist regime and democracy since 1989.

regiones/polonia/demografia.0.nota.texto: Poland within its present-day borders, which do not match the medieval ones.

regiones/polonia/religiones.0.nota.texto: The Slavs reached the region in the 5th and 6th centuries; the name of the Polans appears in the 10th century.

regiones/polonia/religiones.2.nota.texto: From the 14th century Poland took in Jews expelled from other kingdoms; in the early modern period it was the center of Ashkenazi Judaism.

regiones/polonia/culturas.0.nota.texto: Farmers who descended mostly from those of Anatolia, mixed with local hunter-gatherers (Haak et al. 2015).

regiones/polonia/culturas.3.nota.texto: The Pomeranian culture, with its face urns, occupies the north from the 7th century BC.

regiones/polonia/culturas.4.nota.texto: Known only through archaeology: there are no inscriptions or ancient authors who name them here.

regiones/polonia/culturas.5.nota.texto: Przeworsk is usually identified with the Vandals or Lugii of the Roman sources, and Wielbark with the Goths whom Jordanes (Getica) has leave Scandinavia; the ethnic identification of archaeological cultures is debated.

regiones/polonia/culturas.6.nota.texto: The Slavs arrive in the region in the 5th and 6th centuries; the name of the Polans appears in the 10th century.

regiones/polonia/idiomas.0.nota.texto: Nobody knows what languages the Neolithic farmers spoke: they left no texts. regiones/polonia/idiomas.1.nota.texto: No texts. regiones/polonia/idiomas.2.nota.texto: It is inferred from the Roman sources and from Jordanes; there are no texts from the region.

regiones/polonia/idiomas.3.nota.texto: The Slavs arrive in the region in the 5th and 6th centuries; the name of the Polans appears in the 10th century.

regiones/bohemia/resumen.texto: The Czech lands, ringed by mountains in the heart of Europe. Great Moravia received Cyril and Methodius, under Charles IV Prague was the capital of the Empire and the seat of the first university in Central Europe, and in the 15th century, with the Hussites, Bohemia was the first country to break with Rome.

regiones/bohemia/eras.8.nombre.texto: The Luxembourgs and Prague's golden age

regiones/bohemia/eras.0.resumen.texto: Band pottery from around 5500 BC; in the Chalcolithic, Corded Ware and Bell Beaker.

regiones/bohemia/eras.1.resumen.texto: The Únětice culture, which takes its name from a site near Prague; then barrows and urnfields.

regiones/bohemia/eras.2.resumen.texto: The Bylany culture, with chariot burials.

regiones/bohemia/eras.3.resumen.texto: La Tène Celts with oppida such as Závist and Stradonice; the name Bohemia comes from the Boii (Boiohaemum, Tacitus, Germania 28). In the 1st century BC they leave the region or mix with the Germans.

regiones/bohemia/eras.4.resumen.texto: Marbod leads the Marcomanni to Bohemia around 9-6 BC and forms a powerful kingdom; then come the Marcomannic Wars against Rome (166-180) and the great migration.

regiones/bohemia/eras.5.resumen.texto: Slavs settled from the 6th century, under pressure from the Avars and the Franks.

regiones/bohemia/eras.6.resumen.texto: The first Western Slavic state, where Cyril and Methodius created a liturgy in Slavonic; it fell to the Hungarians.

regiones/bohemia/eras.7.resumen.texto: Dukes and then kings of Bohemia within the Holy Roman Empire, with German colonization and silver mines.

regiones/bohemia/eras.8.resumen.texto: Charles IV made Prague the capital of the Empire and founded its university.

regiones/bohemia/eras.9.resumen.texto: The Hussite wars and the forced coexistence of Catholics and Utraquists.

regiones/bohemia/eras.10.resumen.texto: After the defeat at the White Mountain (1620) Catholicism was imposed.

regiones/bohemia/eras.11.resumen.texto: Independent state from 1918, occupied by Germany, communist and separated from Slovakia in 1993.

regiones/bohemia/religiones.0.nota.texto: Enclosures such as Libenice (4th-3rd centuries BC), whose interpretation as a sanctuary is debated.

regiones/bohemia/religiones.2.nota.texto: The Slavs settled in Bohemia around 550; before them the Boii (Celts) and the Marcomanni (Germanic) lived there.

regiones/bohemia/culturas.0.nota.texto: Farmers who descended mostly from those of Anatolia, mixed with local hunter-gatherers (Haak et al. 2015).

regiones/bohemia/culturas.7.nota.texto: Tacitus (Germania 28) says that the name Boiohaemum still recalled the Boii, although the land had changed its inhabitants.

regiones/bohemia/culturas.8.nota.texto: Velleius Paterculus (II.108-109) and Strabo (VII.1.3) recount Marbod's move.

regiones/bohemia/culturas.9.nota.texto: The Slavs settled in Bohemia around 550; before them the Boii (Celts) and the Marcomanni (Germanic) lived there.

regiones/bohemia/idiomas.5.nombre.texto: Church Slavonic (liturgy of Methodius and Sázava)

regiones/bohemia/idiomas.2.nota.texto: No local inscriptions: only names of people, peoples and places transmitted by Greek and Latin authors (Boii, Boiohaemum). The first mention of the Boii in this area is from Posidonius (in Strabo VII.2.2), who recounts that they repelled the Cimbri around 120 BC; that they spoke Celtic earlier is inferred from La Tène archaeology.

regiones/bohemia/idiomas.4.nota.texto: The Slavs settled in Bohemia around 550; before them the Boii (Celts) and the Marcomanni (Germanic) lived there.

regiones/hungria/resumen.texto: The kingdom of the Carpathian Basin, comprising present-day Hungary, Slovakia and Transylvania. The Hungarians, a steppe people speaking a Uralic language, arrived in 895 and became a Christian kingdom c. 1000; it was a frontier of Latin Christendom against the Mongols and the Ottomans.

regiones/hungria/eras.8.nombre.texto: Angevins, Sigismund, Hunyadi and the Jagiellonians

regiones/hungria/eras.0.resumen.texto: Agriculture arrives with the Starčevo-Körös culture around 6000 BC; band pottery originates in western Hungary around 5500 BC; then Lengyel, Tisza and the first copper objects.

regiones/hungria/eras.1.resumen.texto: On the plain there were already kurgans of steppe herders (Yamnaya) from around 3000 BC; in the Bronze Age, settlements on tells and hills (Nagyrév, Vatya, Otomani-Füzesabony), barrows and urnfields.

regiones/hungria/eras.2.resumen.texto: Hallstatt in the west; on the plain, the Vekerzug culture, which is usually linked with the Scythians.

regiones/hungria/eras.3.resumen.texto: From the 4th century BC Celts arrive: Boii, Eravisci, Taurisci and Cotini, with oppida at Bratislava and on Gellért Hill in Budapest. In the mid-1st century BC the Dacians of Burebista defeat the Boii and Taurisci (Strabo VII.3.11 and VII.5.2); Rome conquers Pannonia between 35 and 9 BC.

regiones/hungria/eras.4.resumen.texto: A Roman province west of the Danube, with cities such as Aquincum and Sopianae.

regiones/hungria/eras.5.resumen.texto: Center of Attila's empire and then of the Avar khaganate, destroyed by Charlemagne.

regiones/hungria/eras.6.resumen.texto: The Magyars occupied the basin and raided Europe until their defeat at Lechfeld (955).

regiones/hungria/eras.7.resumen.texto: Stephen I and his successors organized a Christian kingdom; in 1241-1242 the Mongols devastated it.

regiones/hungria/eras.8.resumen.texto: A great power with gold mines, which held back the Ottomans until the defeat at Mohács.

regiones/hungria/eras.9.resumen.texto: The centre was Ottoman, the west and north Habsburg, and Transylvania an autonomous principality.

regiones/hungria/eras.10.resumen.texto: A kingdom within the Habsburg monarchy; from 1867, half of Austria-Hungary.

regiones/hungria/eras.11.resumen.texto: The Treaty of Trianon reduced Hungary to a third and divided the rest among its neighbours.

regiones/hungria/demografia.0.nota.texto: Hungary and Slovakia within their present-day borders; Transylvania is counted under Wallachia and Moldavia (Romania).

regiones/hungria/religiones.3.nombre.texto: Celtic cults in the Roman period

regiones/hungria/religiones.6.nombre.texto: Arianism (Gepids, Ostrogoths and other Germanic peoples)

regiones/hungria/religiones.0.nota.texto: No texts from the period: it is inferred from graves and deposits; the names of local gods, such as Teutanus, come from Roman-period inscriptions.

regiones/hungria/religiones.3.nota.texto: Like that of Teutanus, god of the Eravisci, honored at Aquincum as Jupiter Teutanus.

regiones/hungria/religiones.4.nota.texto: Christianity was the official religion of the Empire from 380, but the sources for Pannonia, which was only Transdanubia (the plain east of the Danube was not Roman), are scarce and do not allow measuring how long the traditional cults lasted.

regiones/hungria/religiones.5.nota.texto: The Huns left no texts of their own; their link with Tengrism is a hypothesis drawn from other steppe peoples.

regiones/hungria/religiones.6.nota.texto: The Gepids shared religion and language with the Goths, who were Arians. There is no census of the population, so it is not marked as the majority religion.

regiones/hungria/religiones.7.nota.texto: Poorly documented; it is linked to Tengrism by analogy with other steppe peoples, with no texts confirming it.

regiones/hungria/religiones.8.nota.texto: Slavs settled in Pannonia and the Carpathians under Avar and then Frankish rule.

regiones/hungria/religiones.9.nota.texto: After the Frankish campaigns against the Avars (791–796), missionaries from Salzburg arrived; later, those from Great Moravia.

regiones/hungria/culturas.0.nota.texto: Farmers who descended mostly from those of Anatolia, mixed with local hunter-gatherers (Haak et al. 2015).

regiones/hungria/culturas.4.nota.texto: Their attribution to the Scythians, or to the Sigynnae that Herodotus (V.9) places north of the Danube, is debated.

regiones/hungria/culturas.8.nota.texto: The Pannonian tombstones of the 1st and 2nd centuries show Celtic names and dress.

regiones/hungria/culturas.9.nota.texto: The Hunnic Empire included many peoples; the origin of the Huns themselves is disputed.

regiones/hungria/culturas.10.nota.texto: How much of the Romanized population remained in Pannonia after 433 is disputed; the written sources are scarce.

regiones/hungria/culturas.11.nota.texto: After Nedao (454), Gepids and Ostrogoths settled in the middle Danube basin; the Lombards occupied Pannonia from around 526 and moved to Italy in 568.

regiones/hungria/culturas.12.nota.texto: The Avars dominated the Carpathian basin from 567 until the early 9th century (Frankish campaigns of 791–796); their origin is disputed (they are linked to the Rouran).

regiones/hungria/idiomas.0.nota.texto: Nobody knows what languages the Neolithic farmers spoke: they left no texts. They are assumed to predate the Indo-European ones because genetics shows that these arrived later, with people of Steppe ancestry; their traces are sought in place names and loanwords, with much-disputed theories.

regiones/hungria/idiomas.1.nota.texto: No texts. That they were Indo-European is inferred from the arrival of people of Steppe ancestry (Haak et al. 2015; Olalde et al. 2018) and from the fact that the first documented languages of the area are Indo-European; when and where Proto-Celtic arose is debated (Koch and Cunliffe: the Atlantic in the Bronze Age; Sims-Williams 2020: Bronze Age Gaul, between the centre and the west of Europe).

regiones/hungria/idiomas.2.nota.texto: Names and coin legends, such as those of BIATEC minted in Bratislava in the 1st century BC.

regiones/hungria/idiomas.6.nota.texto: Only proper names survive in Greek and Latin sources. There is no consensus on its classification (Turkic, Mongolic, Tungusic, Yeniseian, Iranian), and some regard it as unclassifiable. According to Priscus, Gothic was also spoken.

regiones/hungria/idiomas.7.nota.texto: How many people went on speaking it after 433 is disputed.

regiones/hungria/idiomas.8.nota.texto: Gepid resembled Gothic; there are almost no texts.

regiones/hungria/idiomas.9.nota.texto: Almost no texts survive; the khaganate lasted until the early 9th century. It should not be confused with the Avar language of the Caucasus, with which it perhaps has no relation.

regiones/hungria/idiomas.12.nota.texto: Latin was the official language of administration, justice and the Diet of Hungary until 1844.

regiones/balcanes/resumen.texto: The lands between the Adriatic and the Black Sea north of Greece: Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia, Serbia, Montenegro, Albania, North Macedonia, Bulgaria and European Thrace. Settled by Slavs from the 6th century, they were the stage for the Bulgarian empires, Serbia and the Ottoman expansion; Croatia and Slovenia followed Rome and the rest followed Constantinople.

regiones/balcanes/eras.7.nombre.texto: Second Bulgarian Empire, Serbia and Bosnia

regiones/balcanes/eras.0.resumen.texto: The first farmers in Europe outside Greece (Starčevo, Karanovo), the Vinča culture and the gold of the Varna necropolis (around 4500 BC).

regiones/balcanes/eras.1.resumen.texto: Kurgans of steppe herders in the east, fortified settlements and contact with the Mycenaean world in the south.

regiones/balcanes/eras.2.resumen.texto: Thracians in the east, Illyrians in the west and Greek cities on the coasts; the Odrysians form a kingdom in the 5th century BC. After the invasion of 279 BC, the Scordisci settle along the Danube and the Celts of Tylis dominate part of Thrace.

regiones/balcanes/eras.3.resumen.texto: Illyricum, Moesia and Thrace, provinces of the Empire and then of Byzantium.

regiones/balcanes/eras.4.resumen.texto: Slavs and Avars crossed the Danube and occupied almost the whole peninsula.

regiones/balcanes/eras.5.resumen.texto: The Bulgars, a Turkic people who mixed with the Slavs, created an empire that adopted Christianity and the Slavic script.

regiones/balcanes/eras.6.resumen.texto: Basil II the Bulgar-Slayer annexed Bulgaria; Croatia united with Hungary in 1102.

regiones/balcanes/eras.7.resumen.texto: Bulgaria was reborn in Tarnovo and Serbia reached its height with Stephen Dušan.

regiones/balcanes/eras.8.resumen.texto: The Ottomans conquered Bulgaria (1396), Serbia (1459) and Bosnia (1463).

regiones/balcanes/eras.9.resumen.texto: Independence of Serbia and Bulgaria, Yugoslavia and the present-day states.

regiones/balcanes/demografia.0.nota.texto: Sum of Serbia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Albania, Bulgaria, Slovenia and Kosovo.

regiones/balcanes/religiones.0.nota.texto: We know it from Greek authors (Herodotus V.7 names its gods with Greek names: Ares, Dionysus, Artemis and Hermes), from royal tombs such as those of Kazanlak and Sveshtari and from the reliefs of the “Thracian Horseman” of the Roman period.

regiones/balcanes/religiones.2.nota.texto: From the Roman conquest of Illyria (168 BC); before that, Thracian, Illyrian and Greek religions.

regiones/balcanes/religiones.5.nota.texto: Bulgaria was baptized in 864 under Boris I and Serbia in the 9th century.

regiones/balcanes/culturas.5.nombre.texto: Celtic (Scordisci and the kingdom of Tylis)

regiones/balcanes/culturas.0.nota.texto: Farmers who descended mostly from those of Anatolia, mixed with local hunter-gatherers (Haak et al. 2015).

regiones/balcanes/culturas.2.nota.texto: Herodotus (V.3) says that the Thracians were, after the Indians, the most numerous people in the world.

regiones/balcanes/culturas.4.nota.texto: From the Greek colonies on the coast (7th century BC).

regiones/balcanes/culturas.5.nota.texto: The Scordisci, centered on Singidunum (Belgrade), raided Macedonia and Greece until Rome subdued them in the time of Augustus; ancient authors call them Celts, Thracians or Illyrians, and whether they were a Celtic people or a mixed group is debated. The kingdom of Tylis, in Thrace, ends around 212 BC (Polybius IV.46).

regiones/balcanes/culturas.6.nota.texto: From the Roman conquest of Illyria (168 BC); Romanization advanced over the centuries.

regiones/balcanes/idiomas.0.nota.texto: Nobody knows what languages the Neolithic farmers spoke: they left no texts. They are assumed to predate the Indo-European ones because genetics shows that these arrived later, with people of Steppe ancestry; their traces are sought in place names and loanwords, with much-disputed theories.

regiones/balcanes/idiomas.1.nota.texto: No texts. That they were Indo-European is inferred from the arrival of people of Steppe ancestry (Haak et al. 2015; Olalde et al. 2018) and from the fact that the first documented languages of the area are Indo-European; when and where Proto-Celtic arose is debated (Koch and Cunliffe: the Atlantic in the Bronze Age; Sims-Williams 2020: Bronze Age Gaul, between the centre and the west of Europe).

regiones/balcanes/idiomas.2.nota.texto: From the Greek colonies on the coast (7th century BC).

regiones/balcanes/idiomas.3.nota.texto: Very few inscriptions, such as the Ezerovo ring (5th century BC), which no one translates with certainty; it was spoken in the interior until the end of antiquity.

regiones/balcanes/idiomas.4.nota.texto: Known only from names, with no texts. Whether Albanian descends from it is debated.

regiones/balcanes/idiomas.6.nota.texto: From the Roman conquest of Illyria (168 BC); Romanization advanced over the centuries.

regiones/balcanes/idiomas.10.nota.texto: Byzantine sources name the Albanians from 1043 (Michael Attaleiates); the language is older and has been written since 1462.

regiones/rumania/resumen.texto: The lands north of the Danube and east of the Carpathians, ancient Dacia. After centuries of steppe peoples passing through, the principalities of Wallachia and Moldavia, Orthodox and Romance-speaking, emerged in the 14th century; they resisted Ottoman suzerainty and later accepted it.

regiones/rumania/eras.0.resumen.texto: Starčevo-Criș and, in the Chalcolithic, Cucuteni (Trypillia) and Gumelnița, with some of the largest villages of their time in Europe.

regiones/rumania/eras.1.resumen.texto: Steppe herders arrive and bury their dead in kurgans (Yamnaya); in the Bronze Age, the Monteoru, Tei and Noua cultures.

regiones/rumania/eras.2.resumen.texto: Herodotus (IV.93) names the Getae when recounting Darius's campaign (around 514 BC); Burebista brings together a large kingdom around 60-44 BC and Decebalus is defeated by Trajan in 106.

regiones/rumania/eras.3.resumen.texto: Trajan conquered Dacia; Aurelian withdrew the legions south of the Danube.

regiones/rumania/eras.4.resumen.texto: Goths, Huns, Avars, Slavs, Bulgars, Pechenegs, Cumans and Mongols crossed or dominated the plain.

regiones/rumania/eras.5.resumen.texto: Basarab I founded Wallachia (1330) and Bogdan I Moldavia (1359); Vlad III and Stephen the Great resisted the Ottomans.

regiones/rumania/eras.6.resumen.texto: Governed by local princes and then by Phanariote Greeks, they paid tribute to the sultan.

regiones/rumania/eras.7.resumen.texto: Union of the principalities, independence (1878) and Greater Romania (1918).

regiones/rumania/demografia.0.nota.texto: Romania (with Transylvania) and Moldova within their present-day borders.

regiones/rumania/religiones.0.nombre.texto: Religion of the Getae and Dacians

regiones/rumania/religiones.0.nota.texto: Herodotus (IV.94-96) says that the Getae believed that at death they would go to their god Zalmoxis, and interprets it in the Greek manner.

regiones/rumania/religiones.2.nota.texto: Poorly documented: the Goths north of the Danube kept their cults while Arian Christianity advanced (Ulfilas's mission, 341–348; persecution under Athanaric, 369–372).

regiones/rumania/religiones.3.nota.texto: Ulfilas, bishop of the Goths, worked among them from 341 to 348, until a persecution drove him into Moesia. Athanaric persecuted Gothic Christians again in 369–372.

regiones/rumania/religiones.4.nota.texto: The Huns left no texts of their own; their link with Tengrism is a hypothesis drawn from other steppe peoples.

regiones/rumania/religiones.5.nota.texto: Procopius (around 550) reports that the Slavs worshipped a god of lightning as lord of all; the Sclaveni lived north of the Danube (Jordanes, 551).

regiones/rumania/religiones.6.nota.texto: Their presence north of the Danube after 271 is disputed (the debate over Daco-Roman continuity); that is why it comes after the others.

regiones/rumania/culturas.0.nota.texto: Farmers who descended mostly from those of Anatolia, mixed with local hunter-gatherers (Haak et al. 2015).

regiones/rumania/culturas.2.nota.texto: Before Herodotus there is only archaeology; linking the early Iron Age cultures with the Getae is an inference.

regiones/rumania/culturas.4.nota.texto: Carpi and other peoples east of the Carpathians.

regiones/rumania/culturas.5.nota.texto: The Sântana de Mureș–Chernyakhov culture, of the 2nd to 5th centuries, results from a mixture of Goths, Getodacians and Sarmatians; its association with the Goths was much disputed until recent methodological advances.

regiones/rumania/culturas.6.nota.texto: Rule of the Hunnic Empire over the region; the ethnic origin of the Huns is disputed.

regiones/rumania/culturas.7.nota.texto: Jordanes (551) places the Sclaveni between the Dniester, the Vistula and the Danube; the Antes, linked to the Penkovka culture, lived further east.

regiones/rumania/culturas.8.nota.texto: The Avars dominated the Carpathian basin from 567; their origin is disputed (they are linked to the Rouran).

regiones/rumania/culturas.12.nota.texto: Aurelian withdrew Roman administration from Dacia around 271, and Moldavia was never a Roman province. How much of the Romanized population remained north of the Danube is the center of the debate on the origin of the Romanians (Daco-Roman continuity versus the immigrationist theory). Its weight is uncertain, and the Cambridge History of the Romance Languages (2013) concluded that the data are not enough to decide it. That is why it carries less weight and comes last.

regiones/rumania/idiomas.0.nota.texto: Nobody knows what languages the Neolithic farmers spoke: they left no texts. They are assumed to predate the Indo-European ones because genetics shows that these arrived later, with people of Steppe ancestry; their traces are sought in place names and loanwords, with much-disputed theories.

regiones/rumania/idiomas.1.nota.texto: No texts. That they were Indo-European is inferred from the arrival of people of Steppe ancestry (Haak et al. 2015; Olalde et al. 2018) and from the fact that the first documented languages of the area are Indo-European; when and where Proto-Celtic arose is debated (Koch and Cunliffe: the Atlantic in the Bronze Age; Sims-Williams 2020: Bronze Age Gaul, between the centre and the west of Europe).

regiones/rumania/idiomas.2.nota.texto: Almost without texts: names of people and places, and names of medicinal plants recorded by Dioscorides. Whether Dacian was the same language as Thracian is debated.

regiones/rumania/idiomas.3.nota.texto: Until Aurelian withdrew the administration of Dacia (around 271). Moldavia was never a Roman province.

regiones/rumania/idiomas.5.nota.texto: Language of the Goths who dominated the region; almost no texts survive apart from the Gothic Bible, which is linked to the Goths of Moesia.

regiones/rumania/idiomas.6.nota.texto: Only proper names survive in Greek and Latin sources; there is no consensus on its classification.

regiones/rumania/idiomas.7.nota.texto: The Slavic presence north of the Danube is documented (Jordanes around 551, Procopius); it is not known what proportion of the population spoke each language.

regiones/rumania/idiomas.8.nota.texto: Reconstructed Romance language spoken by the ancestors of the Romanians, between the 6th–7th and the 10th–11th centuries. Its presence north of the Danube is inferred and disputed: where it formed, north or south of the Danube, is uncertain, and the Oxford Guide to the Romance Languages (2016) says it is not known. The Slavic presence, by contrast, is documented.

regiones/rumania/idiomas.10.nota.texto: The principalities used Church Slavonic in the Church and in documents until the 17th century.

regiones/rumania/idiomas.11.nota.texto: How much of the Romanized population continued speaking Latin north of the Danube after 271 is the center of the debate on the origin of the Romanians (Daco-Roman continuity versus the immigrationist theory). The Cambridge History of the Romance Languages (2013) concluded that the data are not enough to decide it.

regiones/baltico/resumen.texto: The eastern coast of the Baltic, inhabited by Baltic and Finnic peoples. It was the last pagan region of Europe: the Teutonic and Livonian Orders conquered it through crusades in the 13th century, while Lithuania resisted, expanded to the Black Sea and was baptized in 1386.

regiones/baltico/eras.0.resumen.texto: Prussians, Curonians, Latvians, Lithuanians and Estonians, with the amber trade and contacts with Vikings and Russians.

regiones/baltico/eras.1.resumen.texto: The military orders conquered Livonia and Prussia; the Grand Duchy of Lithuania became a great pagan power.

regiones/baltico/eras.2.resumen.texto: Union of Lithuania with Poland and decline of the Teutonic Order after Grunwald.

regiones/baltico/eras.3.resumen.texto: Livonia was divided between Sweden and Poland and later passed to Russia.

regiones/baltico/eras.4.resumen.texto: The whole region fell into the hands of Russia and Prussia.

regiones/baltico/eras.5.resumen.texto: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania independent, annexed by the USSR and free since 1991.

regiones/baltico/religiones.0.nota.texto: Tacitus describes the Aestii in AD 98; they had lived there long before.

regiones/baltico/religiones.2.nota.texto: Livonia and Prussia were Christianized by force in the 13th century; Lithuania was baptized in 1387 and Samogitia in 1413.

regiones/baltico/culturas.0.nota.texto: Tacitus describes the Aestii in AD 98; they had lived there long before.

regiones/baltico/idiomas.4.nombre.texto: Ruthenian (chancery of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania)

regiones/baltico/idiomas.0.nota.texto: Tacitus describes the Aestii in AD 98; they had lived there long before.

regiones/baltico/idiomas.1.nota.texto: Tacitus describes the Aestii in AD 98; they had lived there long before.

regiones/rus/resumen.texto: The lands of the East Slavs, from Kiev to Novgorod and Moscow: present-day Ukraine, Belarus and European Russia. Kievan Rus' adopted Byzantine Christianity in 988; after the Mongol invasion of 1240 the west passed to Lithuania and Poland, and Moscow grew in the northeast.

regiones/rus/eras.3.nombre.texto: Grand Duchy of Moscow and Tsardom of Russia

regiones/rus/eras.0.resumen.texto: Slavic, Finnic and Baltic tribes in the forests, with Scandinavian traders on the rivers toward Byzantium and the caliphate.

regiones/rus/eras.1.resumen.texto: A federation of principalities ruled by the Rurik dynasty, with Kiev as its capital and the Orthodox Church.

regiones/rus/eras.2.resumen.texto: The Russian principalities paid tribute to the Mongols; Lithuania conquered Kiev and the west, and Moscow became the center of the northeast.

regiones/rus/eras.3.resumen.texto: Muscovy unified the Russian lands and proclaimed itself the heir of Byzantium.

regiones/rus/eras.4.resumen.texto: Peter the Great and his successors made Russia a great European power.

regiones/rus/eras.5.resumen.texto: Revolution, the Soviet Union and independent states since 1991.

regiones/rus/demografia.0.nota.texto: All of Russia (with Siberia and the North Caucasus), Ukraine and Belarus: the country series does not allow separating historical Rus', the steppe or Siberia.

regiones/rus/religiones.0.nota.texto: Procopius (around 550) says the Slavs worshipped a god of lightning as lord of all. Before that there are no sources on the beliefs of the region, nor of the Goths of Chernyakhov or the Huns; that is why 410–499 has no data.

regiones/rus/religiones.1.nota.texto: The Baltic peoples of the Dnieper lived in the forest (Dnieper Balts); there are no sources from the period on their beliefs, and what is known of their religion is an inference from later testimonies.

regiones/rus/religiones.2.nota.texto: The northern Finno-Ugric peoples (Dyakovo culture) left no texts; what is known of their religion is an inference from later testimonies.

regiones/rus/religiones.3.nota.texto: The East Slavs settled the region between the 6th and 8th centuries.

regiones/rus/culturas.0.nota.texto: From 410 to 500 the Slavic evidence rests on the Kiev culture (3rd–5th centuries), the first archaeological culture identifiable as Slavic; from the 6th century, on the Penkovka culture, identified with the Antes, and on the Prague-Korchak culture, identified with the Sclaveni. Attributing ethnic groups to archaeological cultures is disputed.

regiones/rus/culturas.1.nota.texto: The forest zone was Baltic (Dnieper Balts); the Kolochin culture is attributed either to Balts or to Slavs.

regiones/rus/culturas.2.nota.texto: The Dyakovo culture, of the Moskva, Oka and Volga rivers, is one of the oldest known Finno-Ugric cultures; how much Baltic influence weighed on it is disputed.

regiones/rus/culturas.3.nota.texto: The East Slavs settled the region between the 6th and 8th centuries.

regiones/rus/idiomas.5.nombre.texto: Northern Finnic languages (Karelian, Veps and others)

regiones/rus/idiomas.0.nota.texto: No texts; what is known is reconstruction, and the names of the Antes and the Sclaveni from Jordanes and Procopius.

regiones/rus/idiomas.1.nota.texto: No texts; they are inferred from river names and from the Kolochin culture, which is attributed to Balts or to Slavs.

regiones/rus/idiomas.2.nota.texto: No texts; associated with the Dyakovo culture, one of the oldest known Finno-Ugric cultures.

regiones/rus/idiomas.3.nota.texto: The East Slavs settled the region between the 6th and 8th centuries.

regiones/rus/idiomas.5.nota.texto: The Primary Chronicle (attributed to Nestor) names the Chuds and the Ves (Veps) in 862; they had lived there long before.

regiones/sicilia/resumen.texto: The largest island in the Mediterranean, together with Malta. Greek, Roman, Byzantine, Arab and Norman, in the Middle Ages it was a meeting place of Latin, Greek and Arabic cultures: al-Idrisi and the translators of Frederick II worked at the court of Palermo.

regiones/sicilia/eras.0.resumen.texto: Greek colonies such as Syracuse and Agrigento, and Phoenician and Carthaginian cities in the west.

regiones/sicilia/eras.1.resumen.texto: Rome's first province, the granary of the city.

regiones/sicilia/eras.2.resumen.texto: The island passed through the hands of the Vandals and of Odoacer and Theodoric.

regiones/sicilia/eras.3.resumen.texto: Reconquered by Belisarius, it was a Greek province; Emperor Constans II resided in Syracuse.

regiones/sicilia/eras.4.resumen.texto: The Aghlabids of Ifriqiya conquered the island between 827 and 902; Palermo was a great Islamic city.

regiones/sicilia/eras.5.resumen.texto: Roger de Hauteville conquered the island and his son Roger II created a trilingual kingdom in 1130.

regiones/sicilia/eras.6.resumen.texto: Frederick II reigned from Palermo and deported the last Muslims to Lucera.

regiones/sicilia/eras.7.resumen.texto: Charles of Anjou ruled until the revolt of the Sicilian Vespers.

regiones/sicilia/eras.8.resumen.texto: The island passed to the Crown of Aragon and later to the Spanish monarchy.

regiones/sicilia/eras.9.resumen.texto: Kingdom of the Two Sicilies and from 1861 part of Italy; Malta was British and has been independent since 1964.

regiones/sicilia/religiones.0.nota.texto: From the founding of Naxos, the first Greek colony in Sicily (734 BC).

regiones/sicilia/religiones.3.nota.texto: The majority in the west and center; the northeast (Val Demone) remained Greek and Christian.

regiones/sicilia/religiones.5.nota.texto: Frederick II deported the last Muslims of Sicily to Lucera in the 1220s and 1240s.

regiones/sicilia/religiones.8.nota.texto: Expelled in 1492-1493 by the kings of Aragon.

regiones/sicilia/culturas.0.nota.texto: From the founding of Naxos, the first Greek colony in Sicily (734 BC).

regiones/sicilia/culturas.8.nota.texto: Jewish communities are documented in Sicily from late Roman times.

regiones/sicilia/idiomas.0.nota.texto: From the founding of Naxos, the first Greek colony in Sicily (734 BC).

regiones/sicilia/idiomas.4.nota.texto: In Malta, the local Arabic evolved into present-day Maltese.

regiones/finlandia/resumen.texto: The land of the Finnic peoples between the Gulf of Bothnia and Karelia. It was part of the kingdom of Sweden from the 12th and 13th centuries until 1809, an autonomous grand duchy of the Russian Empire until 1917, and since then an independent republic. There, in the 19th century, Elias Lönnrot compiled the Kalevala from Karelian oral poetry.

regiones/finlandia/eras.0.resumen.texto: Finnish, Tavastian and Karelian tribes, without a state, trading with Scandinavians and Slavs.

regiones/finlandia/eras.1.resumen.texto: Sweden and Novgorod contest the territory; the Treaty of Nöteborg (1323) sets a first border.

regiones/finlandia/eras.2.resumen.texto: Part of the kingdom of Sweden; the Lutheran Reformation arrives in the 16th century and Mikael Agricola writes the first books in Finnish.

regiones/finlandia/eras.3.resumen.texto: Autonomy within the Russian Empire after the war of 1808-1809; Finnish nationalism is born.

regiones/finlandia/eras.4.resumen.texto: Independence in 1917, civil war in 1918 and wars with the USSR between 1939 and 1944.

regiones/finlandia/religiones.0.nota.texto: Around the turn of the era, Finnic languages are already spoken in southwestern Finland; there is no earlier record.

regiones/finlandia/culturas.0.nota.texto: Around the turn of the era, Finnic languages are already spoken in southwestern Finland; there is no earlier record.

regiones/finlandia/idiomas.0.nota.texto: Around the turn of the era, Finnic languages are already spoken in southwestern Finland; there is no earlier record.

regiones/finlandia/idiomas.1.nota.texto: Around the turn of the era, the ancestors of the Sami already live in Finland; there is no earlier record.

regiones/estepa-pontica/resumen.texto: The grasslands north of the Black Sea and the Caucasus, from the Danube to the Volga. Scythians, Sarmatians, Goths, Huns, Khazars, Pechenegs, Cumans and the Mongols of the Golden Horde passed through them, and on their coasts Greek colonies flourished and, in the Middle Ages, Genoese and Venetian ones. The Russian Empire colonized it from the late 18th century; today it is divided between Ukraine and Russia.

regiones/estepa-pontica/eras.1.nombre.texto: Catacomb, Poltavka and Multi-Cord Ceramic cultures

regiones/estepa-pontica/eras.3.nombre.texto: End of the Bronze Age and the Cimmerians

regiones/estepa-pontica/eras.0.resumen.texto: Early Bronze Age herders with wagons, whom many researchers link to the spread of the Indo-European languages.

regiones/estepa-pontica/eras.1.resumen.texto: After Yamnaya, herders of the Catacomb culture (around 2500–1950 BC) and of the Poltavka culture occupy the steppe. They are joined by the Multi-Cord Ceramic culture (Babyno); cart-based herding remains the basis of their life.

regiones/estepa-pontica/eras.2.resumen.texto: The successor of Yamnaya, of the Catacomb, Poltavka and Babyno cultures, the Srubna culture (around 1900–1200 BC) buries its dead in log chambers under mounds and spreads from the Volga to the Dnieper. It is usually associated with speakers of Iranian languages, which cannot be proven without texts.

regiones/estepa-pontica/eras.3.resumen.texto: According to Herodotus (5th century BC), the Cimmerians lived on this steppe and the Scythians displaced them; Assyrian records, by contrast, place them south of the Caucasus. It is not known which archaeological culture corresponds to them, and they left no writings.

regiones/estepa-pontica/eras.4.resumen.texto: The Scythians dominate the steppe; the Greeks found Olbia, Panticapaeum and Chersonesos on the coast.

regiones/estepa-pontica/eras.5.resumen.texto: The Sarmatians succeed the Scythians; the Bosporan kingdom, in Crimea, falls into Rome's orbit, and in the 3rd century the Goths arrive.

regiones/estepa-pontica/eras.6.resumen.texto: From the arrival of the Huns, around 375, a succession of steppe peoples follows: Huns, Avars and the Great Bulgaria of Kubrat.

regiones/estepa-pontica/eras.7.resumen.texto: The Khazars, whose elite adopted Judaism, dominate from the Volga to Crimea until Sviatoslav of Kiev defeats them in 965–969.

regiones/estepa-pontica/eras.8.resumen.texto: Nomadic Turkic peoples: the Pechenegs and, from the mid-11th century, the Cumans or Polovtsians, rivals of Rus'.

regiones/estepa-pontica/eras.9.resumen.texto: After the Mongol invasion the steppe is the center of the Golden Horde; Genoa and Venice trade from Caffa and Tana.

regiones/estepa-pontica/eras.10.resumen.texto: The Crimean Tatars, vassals of the Ottoman Empire since 1475, dominate the steppe. Their raids for slaves ravage Poland and Russia, and on the Dnieper the Zaporozhian Cossacks organize.

regiones/estepa-pontica/eras.11.resumen.texto: Russia annexes Crimea in 1783 and colonizes the region; in the 20th century it is divided between Ukraine and Russia, which occupied Crimea in 2014 and invaded Ukraine in 2022.

regiones/estepa-pontica/religiones.2.nom.texto: Tengrism and cults of the Turkic peoples

regiones/estepa-pontica/culturas.3.nota.texto: They arrive around 375 and dominate the steppe until the fall of Attila's empire; their ethnic origin is disputed.

regiones/estepa-pontica/idiomas.2.nota.texto: Only proper names survive in Greek and Latin sources; there is no consensus on its classification.

regiones/cerdena-corcega/resumen.texto: The two large islands of the Tyrrhenian Sea. Sardinia had a civilization of its own, the Nuragic, known for its thousands of stone towers and whose language is unknown; both islands passed through the hands of Carthaginians, Romans, Vandals and Byzantines, and in the Middle Ages Sardinia was divided into four judicates and Corsica came under Pisa and later Genoa. Today Sardinia is part of Italy and Corsica part of France.

regiones/cerdena-corcega/eras.5.nombre.texto: Aragonese and Spanish Sardinia; Genoese Corsica

regiones/cerdena-corcega/eras.6.nombre.texto: Savoyard and Italian Sardinia; French Corsica

regiones/cerdena-corcega/eras.0.resumen.texto: Stone towers (nuraghi) and well sanctuaries in Sardinia; from the 9th century BC, Phoenician colonies such as Nora and Tharros on the coast.

regiones/cerdena-corcega/eras.1.resumen.texto: Carthage controls the coasts of Sardinia; in Corsica, Alalia is contested by Greeks, Etruscans and Carthaginians.
