personas/benito-de-nursia/resumen.texto: He founded the monastery of Monte Cassino c. 529 and wrote the Rule that organized Western monasticism around prayer, work and reading. Benedictine monasteries preserved much of Europe's written culture.

personas/gregorio-magno/resumen.texto: Pope from 590 and one of the four great doctors of the Latin Church. He sent the mission that converted the Anglo-Saxons, and his Moralia on Job and his Dialogues were among the most widely read books of the Middle Ages.

personas/isidoro-de-sevilla/resumen.texto: Archbishop of Seville in the Visigothic kingdom. His Etymologies summarized ancient learning in twenty books and were the standard encyclopedia of the Middle Ages; he also wrote a history of the Goths.

personas/juan-damasceno/resumen.texto: Monk of the monastery of Mar Saba, near Jerusalem, under Arab rule. His Fount of Knowledge systematized Greek theology and, translated into Latin in the 12th century, was used by Peter Lombard and Thomas Aquinas; he defended images against the iconoclasts.

personas/maximo-el-confesor/resumen.texto: Byzantine monk and theologian who maintained that Christ has two wills, divine and human, against imperial religious policy; for this his tongue and right hand were cut off and he died in exile. His synthesis of Christian Neoplatonism influenced Eriugena.

personas/beda/resumen.texto: Monk of Wearmouth-Jarrow, in Northumbria. His Ecclesiastical History of the English People is the main source for Anglo-Saxon England and spread the practice of counting years from the birth of Christ.

personas/alcuino-de-york/resumen.texto: Master of the cathedral school of York, called by Charlemagne to head the palace school. He was the chief promoter of the Carolingian Renaissance: revision of the Bible, teaching of the liberal arts and reform of the schools; he died as abbot of Saint Martin of Tours.

personas/rabano-mauro/resumen.texto: Disciple of Alcuin, abbot of Fulda and archbishop of Mainz. Called the “teacher of Germany”, he wrote the encyclopedia De rerum naturis and manuals for the training of the clergy.

personas/juan-escoto-eriugena/resumen.texto: Irishman who taught at the court of Charles the Bald, in West Francia. He translated Pseudo-Dionysius and Maximus the Confessor from Greek and wrote the Periphyseon, the most ambitious philosophical system of the Early Middle Ages, of Neoplatonic inspiration.

personas/gerberto-de-aurillac/resumen.texto: He studied in Catalonia the science arriving from al-Andalus and, as master of the cathedral school of Reims, spread the abacus with Arabic numerals, the astrolabe and the logic of Boethius. He was pope from 999.

personas/fulberto-de-chartres/resumen.texto: Bishop of Chartres who made its cathedral school one of the most prestigious in France. His letters are a source on feudal obligations.

personas/pedro-damian/resumen.texto: Hermit monk and cardinal, a figure of the Gregorian reform. He distrusted dialectic as opposed to faith and held that divine omnipotence is not subject to the rules of logic.

personas/berengario-de-tours/resumen.texto: Master of Tours who applied dialectic to the Eucharist and denied that the bread and wine changed materially; the controversy with Lanfranc forced a clarification of the doctrine of the real presence.

personas/lanfranco/resumen.texto: Jurist from Pavia who made the abbey of Bec, in Normandy, the most famous school of his time. William the Conqueror made him archbishop of Canterbury in 1070 and reorganized the English Church with him.

personas/anselmo-de-canterbury/resumen.texto: Monk and abbot of Bec and later archbishop of Canterbury. With the motto “faith seeking understanding” he put forward in the Proslogion the ontological argument for the existence of God, and in Cur Deus homo a rational explanation of the Incarnation. He is considered the father of scholasticism.

personas/roscelino/resumen.texto: Master of dialectic considered the first nominalist: universals are merely words (“emissions of the voice”). His application of this idea to the Trinity was condemned at the Council of Soissons in 1092.

personas/anselmo-de-laon/resumen.texto: Master of the school of Laon, the most prestigious in theology at the beginning of the 12th century. His school began the Glossa Ordinaria on the Bible; Abelard mocked him as “a tree with much foliage and no fruit”.

personas/guillermo-de-champeaux/resumen.texto: Master of the cathedral school of Paris and founder of the school of Saint Victor. He defended an extreme realism about universals, which Abelard attacked until he made him change his position.

personas/pedro-abelardo/resumen.texto: The most brilliant dialectician of the 12th century. He proposed an intermediate solution to the problem of universals, arranged the contradictions of the authorities in Sic et non and defended an ethics of intention. His relationship with Heloise and his condemnations at Soissons (1121) and Sens (1141) are famous.

personas/eloisa/resumen.texto: Student and wife of Abelard and later abbess of the Paraclete. Her letters to Abelard, of great classical learning, discuss love, marriage and religious life.

personas/bernardo-de-claraval/resumen.texto: Abbot of Clairvaux and the great promoter of the Cistercian order. A mystic and polemicist, he had Abelard condemned, preached the Second Crusade and inspired the rule of the Templars.

personas/hugo-de-san-victor/resumen.texto: Master of the abbey of Saint Victor in Paris. His Didascalicon is a program of studies that orders all the arts and sciences toward wisdom, and his De sacramentis one of the first theological syntheses.

personas/ricardo-de-san-victor/resumen.texto: Prior of Saint Victor born in Scotland. He wrote on mystical contemplation and a treatise on the Trinity that defines the person as incommunicable existence.

personas/pedro-lombardo/resumen.texto: Master of the cathedral school of Paris and bishop of the city. His four Books of Sentences organized Christian doctrine by topic and were the theology textbook of the universities until the 16th century: every master had to comment on them.

personas/gilberto-porretano/resumen.texto: Master at Chartres and Paris and bishop of Poitiers. His commentaries on Boethius's theological treatises applied a very subtle logic to the Trinity and were examined at the Council of Reims in 1148 at the instigation of Bernard of Clairvaux.

personas/bernardo-de-chartres/resumen.texto: Chancellor of the school of Chartres and a Platonist. John of Salisbury attributes to him the phrase “we are like dwarfs on the shoulders of giants”.

personas/guillermo-de-conches/resumen.texto: Master associated with the school of Chartres. He commented on Plato's Timaeus and explained nature through physical causes, with a theory of elementary particles that earned him the criticism of William of Saint-Thierry.

personas/thierry-de-chartres/resumen.texto: Chancellor of the school of Chartres. He explained the creation account according to Platonic physics and the quadrivium, and gathered the texts of the seven liberal arts in the Heptateuchon.

personas/bernardo-silvestre/resumen.texto: Poet and philosopher of Tours. His Cosmographia narrates in prose and verse the creation of the world and of the human being by Nature, in the Neoplatonic manner of the Timaeus.

personas/juan-de-salisbury/resumen.texto: Student of Abelard, secretary to the archbishops of Canterbury, witness to the murder of Thomas Becket and bishop of Chartres. His Policraticus is the first major medieval treatise of political theory and his Metalogicon describes the schools of his time.

personas/alano-de-lille/resumen.texto: Master in Paris called the “universal doctor”. He wrote the allegorical poems Anticlaudianus and The Plaint of Nature and defended the faith with rational arguments against Cathars, Waldensians, Jews and Muslims.

personas/hildegarda-de-bingen/resumen.texto: Benedictine abbess on the Rhine. She wrote down her visions (Scivias) and works on medicine and natural history, composed liturgical music and corresponded with popes and emperors. She has been a Doctor of the Church since 2012.

personas/joaquin-de-fiore/resumen.texto: Calabrian abbot who divided history into three ages, of the Father, of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and announced the imminent arrival of the third. His ideas inspired the Spiritual Franciscans and many millenarian movements.

personas/adelardo-de-bath/resumen.texto: He traveled through France, Italy, Sicily and the East. He translated Euclid's Elements and the astronomical tables of al-Khwarizmi from Arabic, and in his Natural Questions argued for seeking natural causes before resorting to authority.

personas/gerardo-de-cremona/resumen.texto: The most prolific translator of Toledo: he rendered more than seventy works from Arabic into Latin, among them Ptolemy's Almagest, Avicenna's Canon and treatises by Aristotle, al-Kindi and al-Farabi.

personas/domingo-gundisalvo/resumen.texto: Archdeacon of Cuéllar in Toledo. With Jewish collaborators he translated Avicenna, al-Ghazali and Ibn Gabirol into Latin and wrote De divisione philosophiae, which incorporated the Arabic classification of the sciences.

personas/miguel-escoto/resumen.texto: Scottish translator who in Toledo rendered into Latin commentaries by Averroes and Aristotle's works on animals, and later served as astrologer at the court of Frederick II.

personas/constantino-el-africano/resumen.texto: Physician from North Africa who became a monk at Monte Cassino and translated Arabic medicine into Latin, such as the Pantegni of Ali ibn al-Abbas, the basis of teaching at Salerno.

personas/trota-de-salerno/resumen.texto: 12th-century physician of Salerno, author of a treatise on cures. Her name became attached to the texts on women's medicine known as the Trotula.

personas/guido-de-arezzo/resumen.texto: Monk who invented the staff with lines and spaces and a method for learning to sing at sight, with the syllables ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la taken from a hymn to Saint John.

personas/hroswitha/resumen.texto: Canoness of the Saxon abbey of Gandersheim, the first known woman playwright in Europe. She wrote comedies in Latin in the manner of Terence with female saints as protagonists, legends and a history of Otto I.

personas/leonardo-de-pisa/resumen.texto: He learned Indian and Arabic arithmetic in the port of Bugia, in North Africa. His Liber abaci (1202) spread Hindu-Arabic numerals, zero and commercial arithmetic in Europe; the sequence that bears his name appears in it.

personas/juan-de-sacrobosco/resumen.texto: Master at the University of Paris. His Treatise on the Sphere, a summary of the astronomy of Ptolemy and the Arabs, was the basic astronomy textbook in the universities for four centuries.

personas/pedro-peregrino/resumen.texto: French scholar who in 1269, during the siege of Lucera, described in a letter the poles of the magnet, their attraction and repulsion, and a pivoting compass.

personas/regiomontano/resumen.texto: German astronomer, a disciple of Peuerbach, who completed the Epitome of the Almagest, founded trigonometry as a discipline and set up a press for scientific texts in Nuremberg.

personas/ibn-masarra/resumen.texto: Cordoban philosopher and ascetic, the first thinker of al-Andalus with a system of his own, of Neoplatonic inspiration. His followers were persecuted as heretics.

personas/abulcasis/resumen.texto: Physician at the court of the caliphs of Córdoba. His medical encyclopedia, the Kitab al-Tasrif, has a book on surgery with drawings of more than two hundred instruments that was taught in Europe for centuries.

personas/ibn-hazm/resumen.texto: Cordoban polymath of the Zahiri school of law. He wrote The Ring of the Dove, on love, and a critical history of religions and sects; he was one of the great thinkers of al-Andalus.

personas/azarquiel/resumen.texto: Astronomer of Toledo who invented a universal astrolabe (the azafea) and led the group that prepared the Toledan Tables; he measured the motion of the Sun's apogee.

personas/ibn-gabirol/resumen.texto: Hebrew poet and Andalusi philosopher. His Fountain of Life, written in Arabic and known in Latin as Fons vitae, holds that everything created, even souls, is composed of matter and form; the scholastics believed it to be the work of a Muslim, “Avicebron”.

personas/bahya-ibn-paquda/resumen.texto: Rabbinical judge of Zaragoza. His work in Arabic Duties of the Heart, on the inner life and sincerity before God, was one of the most widely read ethical books of Judaism.

personas/yehuda-halevi/resumen.texto: Hebrew poet of al-Andalus and Castile. In the Kuzari, a dialogue between a Khazar king and sages of each religion, he defended Judaism against Aristotelian philosophy. At the end of his life he traveled to the Holy Land.

personas/abraham-ibn-ezra/resumen.texto: Scholar from Tudela who from 1140 lived as a wanderer through Italy, France and England. His biblical commentaries and his works on astronomy and arithmetic brought Andalusi science to the Jewish communities of Europe.

personas/avempace/resumen.texto: The first great Aristotelian philosopher of al-Andalus. In The Regime of the Solitary he describes how the sage can unite with the intellect even while living in an imperfect city; his criticisms of Aristotle's physics were taken up by Averroes and the scholastics.

personas/avenzoar/resumen.texto: Sevillian physician to the Almoravids and Almohads, a friend of Averroes. His Taysir describes diseases such as pericarditis, and he advocated experimentation and surgery.

personas/ibn-tufail/resumen.texto: Physician and adviser to the Almohad caliphs. His philosophical novel The Self-Taught Philosopher tells how a child raised alone on an island arrives through reason at the knowledge of God. He introduced Averroes to the caliph.

personas/averroes/resumen.texto: Qadi of Córdoba and Seville and physician to the Almohads. His commentaries on almost all of Aristotle's works earned him the name “the Commentator” in the Latin West; in The Incoherence of the Incoherence he defended philosophy against al-Ghazali. His interpretation of the intellect gave rise to Latin Averroism.

personas/abraham-ibn-daud/resumen.texto: The first Aristotelian Jewish philosopher of Sepharad, author of The Exalted Faith and of the Book of Tradition, a chronicle of the Jewish sages. He is usually identified with Avendauth, Gundissalinus's collaborator in the Toledo translations.

personas/maimonides/resumen.texto: Born in Córdoba, he fled the Almohads and settled in Egypt, where he was leader of the Jewish community and physician at Saladin's court. His Mishneh Torah codified Jewish law and his Guide for the Perplexed, written in Arabic, harmonized the Bible with Aristotle; Thomas Aquinas cites him as “Rabbi Moses”.

personas/ibn-arabi/resumen.texto: Sufi mystic born in Murcia who lived in the East from 1202. His doctrine of the unity of being and his Meccan Revelations made him the most influential thinker of Sufism.

personas/ibn-jubayr/resumen.texto: Secretary to the Almohad governor of Granada who made the pilgrimage to Mecca between 1183 and 1185. His travel account describes Egypt, Arabia, Syria, the Crusader States and Norman Sicily.

personas/al-idrisi/resumen.texto: Andalusi geographer trained in Córdoba who worked at the court of the Norman king Roger II of Sicily. His Book of Roger and his silver world map were the most complete geography of his century.

personas/najmanides/resumen.texto: Rabbi of Girona and a central figure of Catalan Judaism. He defended Judaism in the Disputation of Barcelona of 1263 before James I and wrote biblical commentaries with kabbalistic elements; he died in the Holy Land.

personas/abraham-abulafia/resumen.texto: Kabbalist from Zaragoza, founder of prophetic or ecstatic Kabbalah, based on combining the letters of the divine names. He traveled through the East, Italy and Sicily and tried to meet the pope.

personas/moises-de-leon/resumen.texto: Castilian kabbalist to whom the writing of the Zohar, the central work of Kabbalah, is attributed; it is presented as the teachings of the sage Simeon bar Yochai.

personas/gersonides/resumen.texto: Jewish philosopher and astronomer of Provence. In The Wars of the Lord he discussed with Aristotelian rigor creation, providence and divine knowledge of particulars, and invented the “Jacob's staff” to measure angles in the sky.

personas/hasdai-crescas/resumen.texto: Rabbi of Zaragoza and leader of Aragonese Jewry after the attacks of 1391. In The Light of the Lord he criticized Aristotle's physics and admitted the void and the possibility of infinite worlds, ideas later taken up by Spinoza.

personas/joseph-albo/resumen.texto: Aragonese rabbi who defended Judaism in the Disputation of Tortosa (1413-1414). In the Book of Principles he reduced the Jewish faith to three principles: the existence of God, revelation and retribution.

personas/isaac-abravanel/resumen.texto: Financier to the kings of Portugal and to the Catholic Monarchs who tried unsuccessfully to stop the expulsion of the Jews in 1492. In Italy he continued his work as a biblical commentator and philosopher.

personas/roberto-grosseteste/resumen.texto: Master at Oxford, perhaps its first chancellor, and bishop of Lincoln from 1235. He translated Aristotle's Ethics from Greek, commented on the Posterior Analytics and in De luce explained the universe as an expansion of light; he insisted on geometry and experience for the study of nature.

personas/alejandro-de-hales/resumen.texto: English master of theology in Paris who, on becoming a Franciscan in 1236, gave the order its first university chair. He introduced Peter Lombard's Sentences as a teaching text.

personas/guillermo-de-auvernia/resumen.texto: Bishop of Paris and one of the first to discuss Aristotle, Avicenna and Ibn Gabirol in depth, accepting part of their metaphysics and rejecting the eternity of the world.

personas/alberto-magno/resumen.texto: German Dominican known as the “universal doctor”. He commented on almost all of Aristotle's works, integrating Arabic philosophy, and wrote on botany, zoology and minerals based on his own observations. He was the teacher of Thomas Aquinas in Paris and Cologne.

personas/tomas-de-aquino/nacimiento.luga.texto: castle of the counts of Aquino

personas/tomas-de-aquino/resumen.texto: Italian Dominican, master in Paris, Orvieto, Rome and Naples. In the Summa Theologiae and the Summa contra Gentiles he produced the great synthesis of Aristotle and Christian theology: the distinction between essence and existence, the five ways to God and natural law. Canonized in 1323, his doctrine became the reference point of the Catholic Church.

personas/buenaventura/resumen.texto: Franciscan master in Paris and minister general of the order from 1257. From within the Augustinian tradition he subordinated philosophy to theology, and in The Journey of the Mind to God he described the ascent of the soul; he wrote the official biography of Francis of Assisi.

personas/roger-bacon/resumen.texto: English Franciscan, master in Paris and Oxford, known as the “admirable doctor”. Commissioned by Pope Clement IV, he wrote the Opus maius, which defends the study of languages, mathematics, optics and “experimental science” as the basis of all knowledge.

personas/siger-de-brabante/resumen.texto: Master of the faculty of arts in Paris and head of so-called Latin Averroism: following Aristotle and Averroes, he upheld the eternity of the world and the unity of the intellect. His theses were condemned in 1270 and 1277; he died in Orvieto, and Dante placed him in Paradise.

personas/boecio-de-dacia/resumen.texto: Danish master of the faculty of arts in Paris, grammarian and defender of the autonomy of philosophy: he held that the philosopher, reasoning as such, cannot prove that the world had a beginning. He was affected by the condemnation of 1277.

personas/esteban-tempier/resumen.texto: Bishop of Paris who in 1270 condemned thirteen Averroist theses and in 1277, at the pope's request, 219 philosophical and theological propositions, some of them held by Thomas Aquinas.

personas/enrique-de-gante/resumen.texto: Secular master of theology in Paris and member of the commission behind the condemnation of 1277. He defended a metaphysics of essence of Avicennian and Augustinian inspiration; his Quodlibeta were the major reference of the late 13th century.

personas/godofredo-de-fontaines/resumen.texto: Master of theology in Paris, rival of Henry of Ghent. He defended a merely conceptual distinction between essence and existence and criticized the condemnation of 1277 for stifling philosophical discussion.

personas/pedro-de-juan-olivi/resumen.texto: Franciscan from Languedoc, leader of the Spirituals. He defended strict poverty, analyzed the just price and value in contracts, and proposed a theory of impetus for the motion of projectiles.

personas/ramon-llull/resumen.texto: Majorcan who left courtly life to devote himself to converting Muslims and Jews. He devised the Art, a combinatorial method for demonstrating the truths of faith by reason, and wrote in Catalan, Latin and Arabic works such as the Book of the Gentile and the Three Wise Men and Blanquerna.

personas/arnau-de-vilanova/resumen.texto: Physician to kings and popes and master in Montpellier. He wrote widely circulated medical works and spiritual and apocalyptic treatises that brought him into conflict with the theologians of Paris.

personas/vicente-de-beauvais/resumen.texto: Dominican who compiled for Louis IX the Speculum maius, the largest encyclopedia of the Middle Ages, in three parts: nature, doctrine and history.

personas/santiago-de-la-voragine/resumen.texto: Dominican and archbishop of Genoa, author of the Golden Legend, the most widely read collection of saints' lives of the Middle Ages.

personas/juan-duns-escoto/resumen.texto: Scottish Franciscan, master in Oxford, Paris and Cologne, known as the “subtle doctor”. He defended the univocity of being, the primacy of the will, the “thisness” that makes each thing individual, and the immaculate conception of Mary.

personas/meister-eckhart/resumen.texto: German Dominican, master in Paris and preacher in Strasbourg and Cologne. His German sermons on detachment and the birth of God in the soul founded Rhineland mysticism; he died during the proceedings that ended with the condemnation of 28 propositions in 1329.

personas/teodorico-de-freiberg/resumen.texto: German Dominican who explained the primary and secondary rainbow through the refraction and reflection of light inside each drop, with experiments using glass spheres filled with water.

personas/margarita-porete/resumen.texto: Beguine from Hainaut, author of The Mirror of Simple Souls, which describes the annihilation of the soul in divine love. She refused to recant and was burned in Paris in 1310; her book circulated anonymously for centuries.

personas/marsilio-de-padua/resumen.texto: Rector of the University of Paris and author of the Defensor pacis (1324), which grounded law in the community of citizens and denied the pope any coercive power. Condemned, he took refuge at the court of Louis of Bavaria.

personas/guillermo-de-ockham/resumen.texto: English Franciscan, leading representative of nominalism: only individuals exist and universals are signs. His principle of economy, “Ockham's razor”, his logic and his critique of papal power from the court of Louis of Bavaria opened the so-called via moderna.

personas/gualterio-burley/resumen.texto: Master at Oxford and Paris, defender of realism against Ockham. He wrote a widely circulated logic and Lives of the Philosophers.

personas/juan-buridan/resumen.texto: Master of arts in Paris who never moved on to theology. He developed the theory of impetus to explain the motion of projectiles and of the heavens, as well as a highly influential nominalist logic; “Buridan's ass” is a mockery by his critics.

personas/thomas-bradwardine/resumen.texto: Fellow of Merton College, Oxford, and archbishop of Canterbury, killed by the Black Death. In his Treatise on Proportions he formulated a mathematical law of motion, and in De causa Dei he defended divine grace.

personas/gregorio-de-rimini/resumen.texto: Augustinian master in Paris and general of his order. He combined nominalism with a strict doctrine of grace and proposed that the object of knowledge is what is “complexly signifiable” by a proposition.

personas/nicolas-de-autrecourt/resumen.texto: Master in Paris who doubted that the connection between cause and effect or the existence of substances could be proved with certainty. He was forced to burn his writings in 1347.

personas/nicolas-oresme/resumen.texto: Master in Paris and bishop of Lisieux. He represented variable qualities with graphs, discussed the possibility that the Earth rotates, wrote a treatise on money and translated Aristotle into French for Charles V.

personas/juan-wyclif/resumen.texto: Oxford master, a realist in philosophy, who denied the temporal power of the Church and transubstantiation and promoted the first complete translation of the Bible into English. His ideas lived on with the Lollards and with Jan Hus in Bohemia.

personas/jan-hus/resumen.texto: Rector of the University of Prague and preacher at the Bethlehem Chapel. Following Wycliffe, he criticized indulgences and the wealth of the clergy; summoned to the Council of Constance under an imperial safe-conduct, he was condemned and burned, and his death sparked the Hussite Wars.

personas/juan-gerson/resumen.texto: Chancellor of the University of Paris and one of the leading voices at the Council of Constance, which ended the Western Schism. He defended the superiority of the council over the pope and a mystical theology for the laity.

personas/pedro-de-ailly/resumen.texto: Chancellor of Paris and cardinal, defender of the council at Constance. His Imago mundi, a treatise on geography, was read and annotated by Christopher Columbus.

personas/catalina-de-siena/resumen.texto: Tuscan mystic who intervened in the politics of her time and urged the pope to return from Avignon to Rome. Her Dialogue and her letters are classics of the Italian language. She is a Doctor of the Church.

personas/brigida-de-suecia/resumen.texto: Swedish noblewoman who founded the Order of the Most Holy Saviour, with its mother house at Vadstena, and wrote widely read Revelations. She lived in Rome from 1350.

personas/juliana-de-norwich/resumen.texto: Anchoress of Norwich. Her Revelations of Divine Love is the first book in English known to have been written by a woman.

personas/geert-groote/resumen.texto: Preacher from Deventer, founder of the devotio moderna and of the Brethren of the Common Life, who sought an inward and practical piety without taking vows.

personas/tomas-de-kempis/resumen.texto: Canon regular of the devotio moderna in the Low Countries, probable author of the Imitation of Christ, the most widely read devotional book after the Bible.

personas/nicolas-de-cusa/resumen.texto: Cardinal and bishop of Brixen, born in Kues on the Moselle. In On Learned Ignorance he held that God is the coincidence of opposites, unreachable by finite understanding, and that the universe has no fixed center; he also wrote on peace among religions.

personas/focio/resumen.texto: Patriarch of Constantinople and the greatest scholar of his century. His Bibliotheca summarizes and comments on 279 books he had read, many now lost; his conflict with Rome foreshadowed the separation of the Churches.

personas/miguel-pselo/resumen.texto: Byzantine courtier and scholar, “consul of the philosophers” of Constantinople. He revived the study of Plato and the Neoplatonists, and his Chronographia recounts with a personal eye the lives of fourteen emperors and empresses.

personas/juan-italo/resumen.texto: Disciple of Psellos and his successor as consul of the philosophers. In 1082 he was tried and condemned for teaching Platonic doctrines such as the eternity of the world and the pre-existence of souls.

personas/ana-comnena/resumen.texto: Daughter of Emperor Alexios I. In the Alexiad she narrated her father's reign, including the arrival of the First Crusade, with an exceptional philosophical and literary education; she gathered commentators on Aristotle around her.

personas/teodoro-metoquita/resumen.texto: Chief minister of Andronikos II, astronomer and author of philosophical essays. He restored the Chora monastery in Constantinople and decorated it with mosaics.

personas/gregorio-palamas/resumen.texto: Monk of Mount Athos and archbishop of Thessalonica, defender of hesychasm: through contemplative prayer one can see the uncreated light of God, distinct from his essence. His theses were approved at the councils of Constantinople from 1341 to 1351.

personas/barlaam-de-calabria/resumen.texto: Greek monk from Calabria who taught in Constantinople and argued with Palamas over hesychasm. Defeated, he moved to the West and in Avignon taught Greek to Petrarch.

personas/gemisto-pleton/resumen.texto: Byzantine Neoplatonist philosopher from Mystras. At the Council of Florence in 1439 his lectures on the differences between Plato and Aristotle awakened interest in Plato in Italy; he also proposed a pagan philosophical religion in his Book of Laws.

personas/besarion/resumen.texto: Metropolitan of Nicaea who signed the union of the Churches in Florence and remained in Italy as a cardinal. He defended Plato against his critics and donated his Greek manuscripts to Venice, the core of the Biblioteca Marciana.

personas/jorge-de-trebisonda/resumen.texto: Greek humanist born in Crete who translated Aristotle and Ptolemy into Latin and attacked Plato and Plethon, which provoked Bessarion's response.

personas/genadio-escolario/resumen.texto: Byzantine philosopher, admirer of Thomas Aquinas and opponent of union with Rome. He was the first patriarch of Constantinople under the Ottomans and had Plethon's Book of Laws burned.

personas/petrarca/resumen.texto: Poet and scholar regarded as the father of humanism. He searched for and copied manuscripts of classical authors, such as lost letters of Cicero, wrote moral works in Latin and, in Tuscan, the Canzoniere dedicated to Laura.

personas/leonardo-bruni/resumen.texto: Chancellor of Florence and humanist who translated Plato and Aristotle from Greek. His History of the Florentine People is the first modern history of a city, with periods and critically examined sources.

personas/lorenzo-valla/resumen.texto: Roman humanist who demonstrated with philological arguments that the Donation of Constantine was a forgery, criticized scholastic logic and defended Epicurean pleasure in De voluptate. He worked at the court of Alfonso V in Naples.

personas/cosme-de-medici/resumen.texto: Banker who ruled Florence from 1434 without formal office. He protected artists and humanists, collected manuscripts and commissioned Marsilio Ficino to translate Plato.

personas/marsilio-ficino/resumen.texto: Florentine humanist under the protection of the Medici, who gave him a villa at Careggi where he gathered the so-called Platonic Academy. He translated all of Plato, Plotinus and the Corpus Hermeticum into Latin, and in the Platonic Theology he defended the immortality of the soul.

personas/pico-della-mirandola/resumen.texto: Young nobleman who in 1486 proposed to debate in Rome 900 theses drawn from all traditions: scholasticism, Platonism, Kabbalah and Hermeticism. The pope suspended the debate; the speech prepared to open it, the Oration on the Dignity of Man, became a manifesto of the Renaissance.

personas/cristina-de-pizan/resumen.texto: Venetian-born writer raised at the court of Charles V of France. Widowed young, she lived by her pen; in The Book of the City of Ladies she answered the misogyny of authors with a gallery of illustrious women, and she wrote on politics, war and the education of princes.

personas/dante-alighieri/resumen.texto: Florentine poet exiled in 1302 because of factional strife. His Comedy, a journey through Hell, Purgatory and Paradise, sums up the cosmology, philosophy and theology of his time and established the Italian language; in Monarchia he defended the independence of imperial power from the pope.

personas/brunetto-latini/resumen.texto: Florentine notary and chancellor, teacher of Dante. During his exile in France he wrote in French Li Livres dou Trésor, an encyclopedia for laypeople.

personas/giovanni-boccaccio/resumen.texto: Florentine writer, author of the Decameron, a hundred stories told by young people fleeing the plague of 1348. An admirer of Dante and friend of Petrarch, he promoted the study of Greek in Florence.

personas/geoffrey-chaucer/resumen.texto: Official and diplomat of the English court who traveled to Italy and came to know the work of Dante and Boccaccio. His Canterbury Tales made the English of London a literary language.

personas/chretien-de-troyes/resumen.texto: Poet at the court of Marie de Champagne who created the Arthurian romance: Lancelot, Yvain and Perceval, in which the Grail appears for the first time.

personas/guillermo-ix/resumen.texto: Duke of Aquitaine and count of Poitiers, the first troubadour whose poems survive, in the Occitan language.

personas/wolfram-von-eschenbach/resumen.texto: Knight and poet from Franconia, author of Parzival, the great German romance of the Grail.

personas/snorri-sturluson/resumen.texto: Icelandic chieftain and twice lawspeaker of the Althing. He wrote the Prose Edda, a handbook of Norse poetry and mythology, and the Heimskringla, a history of the kings of Norway; he was murdered on the orders of King Haakon IV.

personas/saxo-grammaticus/resumen.texto: Danish cleric in the service of Archbishop Absalon of Lund. His Gesta Danorum, in Latin, tells the history of Denmark from its legendary kings and includes the legend of Amleth, the origin of Hamlet.

personas/ari-thorgilsson/resumen.texto: Icelandic priest known as “the Learned”, author of the Book of the Icelanders, the first history of Iceland written in Old Norse.

personas/gregorio-de-tours/resumen.texto: Bishop of Tours from a Gallo-Roman senatorial family. His Ten Books of Histories, known as the History of the Franks, are the main source for Merovingian Gaul.

personas/jordanes/resumen.texto: Official of Gothic origin who in 551, in Constantinople, wrote the Getica, a summary of Cassiodorus's history of the Goths, now lost.

personas/procopio/resumen.texto: Secretary to the general Belisarius and the great historian of the age of Justinian. He narrated his wars against the Persians, Vandals and Goths, described his buildings and wrote a Secret History full of attacks on the emperor and Theodora.

personas/pablo-el-diacono/resumen.texto: Lombard monk who spent time at the court of Charlemagne and at Montecassino wrote the History of the Lombards, the main source for his people.

personas/eginardo/resumen.texto: Courtier and architect of Charlemagne. His Life of Charlemagne, inspired by Suetonius, is the most important biography of the Early Middle Ages.

personas/dhuoda/resumen.texto: Frankish noblewoman, wife of Bernard of Septimania. For her sixteen-year-old son, handed over as a hostage to Charles the Bald, she wrote a Handbook of moral and religious advice, one of the rare texts by a lay woman of the Carolingian era.

personas/liutprando-de-cremona/resumen.texto: Bishop of Cremona and ambassador of Otto I to the Byzantine emperor. His report on the embassy of 968 is a scathing chronicle of the court of Constantinople.

personas/adan-de-bremen/resumen.texto: Cleric of Bremen who wrote the history of the archbishops of Hamburg and a description of the northern lands, with the temple at Uppsala and the first written mention of Vinland.

personas/nestor-el-cronista/resumen.texto: Monk of the Kiev Monastery of the Caves to whom tradition attributes the Tale of Bygone Years, the first history of Rus'.

personas/cosmas-de-praga/resumen.texto: Dean of Prague Cathedral and author of the Chronicle of the Bohemians, the first history of Bohemia, in Latin.

personas/jan-dlugosz/resumen.texto: Canon of Kraków and tutor to the sons of Casimir IV. His Annals of the Glorious Kingdom of Poland, in twelve books, are the great medieval history of Poland.

personas/geoffrey-de-monmouth/resumen.texto: Cleric from Monmouth, of Welsh or Breton family (this is disputed), who between 1129 and 1151 signs documents in Oxford, probably as a canon of St George's College, and in 1152 was consecrated bishop of St Asaph. His History of the Kings of Britain (around 1136) spread the legend of King Arthur, Merlin and King Lear across Europe.

personas/mateo-de-paris/resumen.texto: Monk of St Albans whose Chronica majora, illustrated by himself with drawings and maps, is the great English chronicle of the 13th century.

personas/villehardouin/resumen.texto: Marshal of Champagne, one of the leaders of the Fourth Crusade. His Conquest of Constantinople is one of the first works of history in French prose.

personas/jean-de-joinville/resumen.texto: Seneschal of Champagne who accompanied Louis IX on the Seventh Crusade. His Life of Saint Louis, dictated at the age of eighty, is an intimate portrait of the king.

personas/jean-froissart/resumen.texto: Chronicler from Hainaut who traveled through the courts of England, France and Scotland. His Chronicles narrate the Hundred Years' War from the perspective of chivalry.

personas/giovanni-villani/resumen.texto: Florentine banker and politician who died in the plague of 1348. His New Chronicle contains exceptional statistics on the population, schools and economy of Florence.

personas/marco-polo/resumen.texto: Venetian merchant who lived for seventeen years in the China of Kublai Khan. His travel book, dictated in a Genoese prison to Rustichello da Pisa, gave Europe its image of Asia.

personas/alfonso-x/resumen.texto: King of Castile and León from 1252. He directed workshops of Christian, Jewish and Muslim scholars who translated and composed in Castilian works of law (the Siete Partidas), history, astronomy (the Alfonsine Tables) and poetry in Galician-Portuguese (the Cantigas).

personas/don-juan-manuel/resumen.texto: Nephew of Alfonso X and one of the most powerful nobles of Castile. His Count Lucanor, fifty tales with a moral, is a masterpiece of medieval Castilian prose.

personas/patricio-de-irlanda/resumen.texto: British missionary who, kidnapped at sixteen and enslaved in Ireland, returned as a bishop to evangelize it in the 5th century. His two Latin writings, the Confessio and the Letter to Coroticus, are the oldest surviving texts written in Ireland apart from the Ogham inscriptions, and they give no dates and do not name Armagh. Before him, in 431, the pope had sent Palladius as the first bishop of the Irish (Prosper of Aquitaine); Patrick's traditional dates (432-461, or his death in 493) and the accounts of Tara, the druids and the fire of Slane come from Muirchú and Tírechán, in the 7th century.

personas/columba/resumen.texto: Irish monk of the northern Uí Néill lineage who founded the monastery of Iona around 563. According to Bede (III.4) he converted the northern Picts; the Life written by Adomnán around 700 shows him visiting the Pictish king Bridei, but does not tell of a conversion, and the extent of his mission is debated. The idea that he left Ireland as a penance for the Battle of Cúl Dreimne (561) comes from traditions later than Adomnán.

personas/columbano/resumen.texto: Irish monk who around 590 went to the continent and founded monasteries in Gaul, such as Luxeuil, and in Italy, such as Bobbio (614), and spread private penance and Irish monastic discipline. Expelled from Burgundy in 610 after clashing with Queen Brunhild, we know him from his letters and from the Life written by Jonas of Bobbio around 640.

personas/teodorico-el-grande/resumen.texto: King of the Ostrogoths who conquered Italy in 493 and governed it from Ravenna with the Roman administration, with Cassiodorus and Boethius among his ministers.

personas/clodoveo-i/resumen.texto: King of the Franks who unified Gaul, defeated the Visigoths at Vouillé (507) and was baptized in the Catholic faith, which gained him the support of the Church and of the Gallo-Roman population.

personas/justiniano-i/resumen.texto: Byzantine emperor who reconquered Italy, North Africa and southern Hispania, ordered the compilation of Roman law in the Corpus iuris civilis and rebuilt Hagia Sophia.

personas/teodora/resumen.texto: Wife of Justinian and empress with power of her own. According to Procopius, her resolve saved the throne during the Nika riots of 532.

personas/recaredo-i/resumen.texto: Visigothic king who abandoned Arianism and converted his people to Catholicism at the Third Council of Toledo (589).

personas/carlos-martel/resumen.texto: Mayor of the palace who governed the Frankish kingdom and defeated an Umayyad army between Tours and Poitiers in 732. His son Pepin became king and his grandson Charlemagne, emperor.

personas/carlomagno/resumen.texto: King of the Franks from 768 and of the Lombards from 774, crowned emperor in Rome in the year 800. He brought almost all of Latin Europe under his rule and, from Aachen, promoted a reform of schools and texts, the Carolingian Renaissance.

personas/carlos-el-calvo/resumen.texto: Grandson of Charlemagne, king of West Francia from the Treaty of Verdun (843) and emperor from 875. His court was a center of learning where John Scotus Eriugena worked.

personas/alfredo-el-grande/resumen.texto: King of Wessex who resisted the Great Viking Army and defeated it at Edington (878). He promoted the translation into Old English of works by Boethius, Gregory the Great, Orosius and Bede.

personas/abderraman-iii/resumen.texto: Umayyad emir of Córdoba who proclaimed himself caliph in 929, subdued the rebels of al-Andalus and built Madinat al-Zahra.

personas/al-hakam-ii/resumen.texto: Caliph of Córdoba who assembled a library of some 400,000 volumes according to the sources and enlarged the Great Mosque.

personas/almanzor/resumen.texto: Hajib (chief minister) of Caliph Hisham II and the real ruler of al-Andalus. He led more than fifty campaigns against the Christian kingdoms, among them the sack of Santiago de Compostela in 997.

personas/oton-i/resumen.texto: King of Germany who defeated the Hungarians at Lechfeld (955) and was crowned emperor in Rome in 962, the origin of the Holy Roman Empire.

personas/vladimiro-i/resumen.texto: Grand prince of Kiev who in 988 was baptized and adopted Byzantine Christianity for his people.

personas/yaroslav-el-sabio/resumen.texto: Grand prince of Kiev at the height of the Rus. He had Saint Sophia of Kiev built, the first version of the Russkaya Pravda is attributed to him, and he married his daughters to the kings of France, Hungary and Norway.

personas/esteban-i-de-hungria/resumen.texto: First king of Hungary, crowned c. 1000. He Christianized the Hungarians, founded bishoprics and organized the kingdom into counties.

personas/mieszko-i/resumen.texto: First historical ruler of Poland, of the Piast dynasty. His baptism in 966 marks the beginning of the Christian Polish state.

personas/canuto-el-grande/resumen.texto: King of England, Denmark and Norway, the North Sea Empire.

personas/brian-boru/resumen.texto: King of Munster from 978 and high king of Ireland from 1002; a note written in his presence in 1005 in the Book of Armagh calls him “emperor of the Irish”. He died in the Battle of Clontarf (1014), where his army defeated the king of Leinster and the Norse kingdom of Dublin, with its allies from Orkney and the Isle of Man. The image of Clontarf as the battle that ended Viking power comes from the Cogad Gáedel re Gallaib, written a century later for his descendants; many historians see it as a war between Irishmen, with Norsemen on both sides.

personas/guillermo-el-conquistador/resum.texto: Duke of Normandy who conquered England after his victory at Hastings (1066). He ordered the survey of the Domesday Book.

personas/gregorio-vii/resumen.texto: Pope who promoted the reform of the Church and asserted papal supremacy in the Dictatus papae. His conflict with Emperor Henry IV began the Investiture Controversy.

personas/enrique-iv-del-sacro-imperio/re.texto: King of Germany and emperor, rival of Gregory VII in the Investiture Controversy. In 1077 he humbled himself before the pope at Canossa to have his excommunication lifted.

personas/urbano-ii/resumen.texto: French pope, a monk of Cluny, who called for the First Crusade at the Council of Clermont (1095).

personas/el-cid/nombre.texto: Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, El Cid

personas/el-cid/resumen.texto: Castilian knight who served Christian and Muslim kings and conquered Valencia in 1094. The Cantar de mio Cid made him the hero of Castile.

personas/alfonso-vi/nombre.texto: Alfonso VI of León and Castile

personas/alfonso-vi/resumen.texto: King of León and Castile who conquered Toledo in 1085 and styled himself “emperor of the two religions”.

personas/roger-ii/resumen.texto: First Norman king of Sicily, whose court in Palermo brought together Latin, Greek and Arab scholars, among them al-Idrisi.

personas/leonor-de-aquitania/resumen.texto: Duchess of Aquitaine, queen of France and later of England, mother of Richard the Lionheart and John Lackland. Her court at Poitiers was a patron of the troubadours.

personas/federico-i-barbarroja/resumen.texto: Emperor who sought to impose his authority on the Italian communes and was defeated at Legnano (1176). He drowned in Anatolia on his way to the Third Crusade.

personas/federico-ii/resumen.texto: King of Sicily and emperor, called “wonder of the world”. His court brought together translators, astrologers and poets; he founded the University of Naples and wrote a treatise on falconry based on observation.

personas/inocencio-iii/resumen.texto: The most powerful pope of the Middle Ages. He called the Fourth Crusade and the Albigensian Crusade, approved the Franciscans and convened the Fourth Lateran Council (1215).

personas/francisco-de-asis/resumen.texto: Son of a merchant of Assisi who chose a life of absolute poverty and founded the Order of Friars Minor. His Canticle of the Creatures is one of the first poems in Italian.

personas/domingo-de-guzman/resumen.texto: Castilian canon who preached against the Cathars in Languedoc and founded in Toulouse the Order of Preachers, the Dominicans, devoted to study and preaching.

personas/luis-ix/resumen.texto: King of France known as Saint Louis. He led two crusades, reformed royal justice and had the Sainte-Chapelle built.

personas/jaime-i/resumen.texto: King of Aragon who conquered Majorca (1229) and Valencia (1238). His Book of Deeds is the first of the great Catalan chronicles.

personas/fernando-iii/resumen.texto: King who permanently united Castile and León and conquered Córdoba (1236), Jaén and Seville (1248).

personas/alejandro-nevski/resumen.texto: Prince of Novgorod and grand prince of Vladimir. He defeated the Swedes on the Neva (1240) and the Teutonic Knights at Lake Peipus (1242), and agreed to submit to the Golden Horde.

personas/felipe-iv-de-francia/resumen.texto: King of France who clashed with Pope Boniface VIII, brought about the move of the papacy to Avignon and destroyed the Order of the Temple.

personas/bonifacio-viii/resumen.texto: Pope who proclaimed the first jubilee (1300) and in the bull Unam sanctam asserted papal supremacy over all power. He was humiliated at Anagni by the envoys of Philip IV.

personas/eduardo-iii/resumen.texto: King of England who claimed the crown of France and began the Hundred Years' War, with the victories of Crécy and Poitiers.

personas/carlos-iv-del-sacro-imperio/res.texto: King of Bohemia and emperor who made Prague a capital: he founded its university (1348) and the New Town. His Golden Bull (1356) set the election of the emperor by seven princes.

personas/casimiro-iii/resumen.texto: Last Piast king of Poland. He codified the laws, founded the University of Kraków (1364) and took in the Jews expelled from other kingdoms.

personas/jogaila/resumen.texto: Grand duke of Lithuania who in 1386 was baptized, married Queen Jadwiga and became king of Poland, uniting the two states. He defeated the Teutonic Order at Grunwald (1410).

personas/margarita-i/resumen.texto: Queen who united Denmark, Norway and Sweden in the Kalmar Union (1397).

personas/juana-de-arco/resumen.texto: Peasant girl from Lorraine who, guided by voices she believed divine, lifted the siege of Orléans in 1429 and brought Charles VII to be crowned at Reims. Captured, she was tried for heresy and burned in Rouen.

personas/jan-zizka/resumen.texto: Hussite military leader, never defeated, who defended Bohemia against the imperial crusades with war wagons and firearms.

personas/juan-gutenberg/resumen.texto: Goldsmith from Mainz who developed printing with movable metal type, with an adapted ink and press. His 42-line Bible, from c. 1455, was the first major printed book in Europe.

personas/constantino-xi/resumen.texto: Last Byzantine emperor, killed defending Constantinople against Mehmed II.

personas/mehmed-ii/resumen.texto: Ottoman sultan who conquered Constantinople in 1453 and made it his capital. He was a patron of Greek and Italian scholars and commissioned his portrait from Gentile Bellini.

personas/matias-corvino/resumen.texto: King of Hungary who formed a standing army, conquered Vienna and assembled in Buda the Bibliotheca Corviniana, one of the largest libraries of its time.

personas/ivan-iii/resumen.texto: Grand prince of Moscow who annexed Novgorod, stopped paying tribute to the Horde (1480) and married the niece of the last Byzantine emperor.

personas/isabel-i/nacimiento.lugar.texto: Monastery of Nuestra Señora de Gracia

personas/isabel-i/resumen.texto: Queen of Castile who, with Ferdinand of Aragon, conquered Granada, imposed the Inquisition, expelled the Jews and supported the voyage of Columbus (1492).

personas/fernando-ii/resumen.texto: King of Aragon and, through his marriage to Isabella, of Castile. Machiavelli took him as a model of a prince in The Prince.

personas/lorenzo-de-medici/resumen.texto: Known as the Magnificent, he ruled Florence and was a patron of Ficino, Pico, Poliziano, Botticelli and the young Michelangelo.

personas/murad-ii/resumen.texto: Ottoman sultan twice, from 1421 to 1444 and from 1446 to 1451, son of Mehmed I. He suppressed rebellions by pretenders backed by Byzantium, besieged Constantinople in 1422 without taking it, annexed Anatolian emirates, took Thessalonica from the Venetians in 1430 and annexed Serbia in 1439. He abdicated in 1444 in favor of his son Mehmed II; that same year, summoned by the grand vizier, he commanded the army that defeated the crusade at Varna. He regained the throne in 1446 and in 1448 defeated John Hunyadi at the second Battle of Kosovo.

personas/bayezid-ii/resumen.texto: Son of Mehmed II, Ottoman sultan from 1481 to 1512. He contested the throne with his brother Cem, who fled to Rhodes and ended up in the hands of Pope Innocent VIII. In 1484 he took the Moldavian ports of Kilia and Akkerman, which made the Black Sea an “Ottoman lake”; in the war with Venice of 1499–1503 he took Lepanto, Modon, Coron and Navarino, and Venice kept Nauplia and Monemvasia until 1540. He welcomed into his lands, especially in Salonica, the Sephardic Jews expelled from Spain in 1492. He defeated a Qizilbash Shiite rebellion backed by Persia and handed the throne to his son Selim I on 24 April 1512, under pressure from the Janissaries and from Selim, who had rebelled; historians debate whether it was voluntary. He died on the way to Didymoteicho and was buried in Istanbul.

personas/enrique-ii-de-champana/resumen.texto: Count of Champagne from 1181, he went on the Third Crusade and reached Acre in July 1190. In April 1192, when the barons of the kingdom chose Conrad of Montferrat as king, he brought him the news, and Conrad was assassinated a few days later. The nobles then chose Henry, who married the heiress Isabella. He governed the kingdom without being crowned, supported by the barons and in tension with the Church, until he died in Acre after falling from a window of his palace.

personas/juan-ii-de-aragon/resumen.texto: King of Navarre from 1425 through his marriage to Blanca, and of Aragon, Sardinia and Sicily (the last until 1468) from 1458, brother and successor of Alfonso V. His reign was marked by the civil war in Navarre against his son Charles of Viana, who died in 1461, and by the Catalan civil war, which ended in 1472. He pawned Roussillon to King Louis XI of France. He arranged the marriage of his son Ferdinand to Isabella of Castile (1469), which led to the union of the two crowns. A Jewish physician operated on his cataracts in 1468.

hechos/saqueo-de-roma-410/resumen.texto: Alaric's Visigoths sacked Rome for three days, the first time in eight centuries that the city had fallen to a foreign enemy. The shock led Augustine to write The City of God.

hechos/reino-visigodo-de-tolosa/resumen.texto: Rome settled the Visigoths as foederati in Aquitaine, with their capital at Toulouse. From there they extended their rule into Hispania.

hechos/campos-catalaunicos/resumen.texto: A coalition of Romans and Visigoths led by Aetius halted Attila's Huns in Gaul. The Visigothic king Theodoric I died in the battle.

hechos/reino-ostrogodo/resumen.texto: Theodoric, sent by the Eastern emperor, defeated Odoacer and took Ravenna. The Ostrogothic kingdom preserved the Roman administration and the Senate.

hechos/batalla-de-vouille/resumen.texto: Clovis defeated the Visigoths of Alaric II, who lost almost all of Gaul and moved their kingdom to Hispania.

hechos/fundacion-de-montecassino/resumen.texto: Benedict of Nursia founded his monastery over an ancient temple of Apollo, atop a mountain between Rome and Naples. There he wrote his Rule.

hechos/cierre-de-la-academia/titulo.texto: Justinian forbids pagans to teach philosophy

hechos/cierre-de-la-academia/resumen.texto: An edict of Justinian forbade pagans to teach. The Neoplatonic school of Athens closed and its last head, Damascius, left with other philosophers for Persia; they returned after a treaty of 532.

hechos/codigo-de-justiniano/resumen.texto: A commission led by Tribonian gathered in a few years the imperial laws and the opinions of the Roman jurists. It became the foundation of European law.

hechos/reconstruccion-de-santa-sofia/res.texto: After the Nika riots, Justinian commissioned Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus to build a new church with a 31-meter dome, the largest in the world for almost a thousand years.

hechos/guerra-gotica/resumen.texto: Justinian reconquered Italy from the Ostrogoths in a war of almost twenty years that ruined the peninsula.

hechos/peste-de-justiniano/resumen.texto: First known great pandemic of bubonic plague, arriving from Egypt. It killed a huge share of the Mediterranean population and returned in waves until the 8th century.

hechos/invasion-lombarda/resumen.texto: The Lombards of King Alboin crossed the Julian Alps and conquered much of Italy, which remained divided between them and the Byzantines until the 8th century.

hechos/iii-concilio-de-toledo/resumen.texto: King Reccared and the Visigothic bishops abandoned Arianism and adopted the Catholic faith, which united Goths and Hispano-Romans.

hechos/mision-gregoriana/resumen.texto: Sent by Gregory the Great, Augustine and forty monks arrived in Kent and baptized King Æthelberht. The Christianization of the Anglo-Saxons began.

hechos/sinodo-de-whitby/resumen.texto: King Oswiu of Northumbria chose the Roman date for Easter and the Roman tonsure over those of the Irish tradition of Iona, which brought the Anglo-Saxon Church closer to Rome. It is told by Bede (III.25) and by the Life of Wilfrid by Stephen of Ripon. It was a dispute over customs, not a schism: the Picts of King Nechtan adopted the Roman Easter around 710-715 (Bede V.21) and Iona itself in 716.

hechos/batalla-de-guadalete/resumen.texto: An Arab and Berber army under Tariq defeated the Visigothic king Roderic. Within a few years almost the entire Peninsula was under Muslim rule.

hechos/batalla-de-covadonga/resumen.texto: A group of Asturians led by Pelagius defeated a Muslim expedition in the Picos de Europa. Later chronicles presented it as the beginning of the Reconquista.

hechos/batalla-de-poitiers-732/resumen.texto: Charles Martel defeated an Umayyad army led by the governor of al-Andalus, Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi, who died in the fighting.

hechos/iconoclasia/resumen.texto: The Byzantine emperors banned the veneration of icons in two periods (726-787 and 814-843). Empress Theodora restored the images in 843, the “Feast of Orthodoxy”.

hechos/emirato-de-cordoba/resumen.texto: Abd al-Rahman I, the last survivor of the Umayyad dynasty overthrown in Damascus, became emir of al-Andalus, independent of the Abbasids of Baghdad.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-mezquita-de-cordo.texto: Abd al-Rahman I began the Great Mosque on the site of the Visigothic basilica of Saint Vincent; his successors enlarged it four times.

hechos/batalla-de-roncesvalles/resumen.texto: The Basques attacked the rearguard of Charlemagne's army on its return from Zaragoza and killed the prefect Roland. The Song of Roland turned the episode into an epic.

hechos/ataque-a-lindisfarne/resumen.texto: The Vikings sacked the monastery of Lindisfarne, the first recorded major Norse raid on the West. Alcuin wrote from Charlemagne's court lamenting it.

hechos/renacimiento-carolingio/resumen.texto: Charlemagne and his successors promoted schools in cathedrals and monasteries, the correction of the Bible and liturgical texts, and the copying of classical authors in the new Carolingian minuscule script.

hechos/coronacion-de-carlomagno/resumen.texto: Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor of the Romans in St. Peter's on Christmas Day of the year 800, restoring the imperial title in the West.

hechos/tratado-de-verdun/resumen.texto: Charlemagne's three grandsons divided the Empire: Charles the Bald received the west, Louis the German the east, and Lothair the center with the imperial title.

hechos/alfabeto-glagolitico/resumen.texto: The brothers Cyril and Methodius, from Thessalonica, arrived in Great Moravia sent by Byzantium. They created the Glagolitic alphabet and translated the liturgy into Slavonic.

hechos/gran-ejercito-pagano/resumen.texto: A great Danish army landed in East Anglia and within a few years conquered Northumbria, East Anglia and part of Mercia. Only Wessex held out.

hechos/batalla-de-edington/resumen.texto: Alfred the Great defeated the Danish leader Guthrum, who was baptized and accepted a division of England: the Danes remained in the Danelaw.

hechos/fundacion-de-cluny/resumen.texto: Duke William of Aquitaine donated land for a monastery free of all lay and episcopal authority, under the direct protection of the pope. It was the center of a great monastic reform.

hechos/fundacion-de-normandia/resumen.texto: King Charles the Simple ceded the region of Rouen to the Viking leader Rollo in exchange for his baptism and his loyalty. Thus Normandy was born.

hechos/califato-de-cordoba/resumen.texto: Abd al-Rahman III proclaimed himself caliph, on the same level as the Abbasids of Baghdad and the Fatimids of Egypt. Córdoba reached its greatest splendor.

hechos/fundacion-del-althing/resumen.texto: The settlers of Iceland created a general assembly that met every summer at Þingvellir to make laws and settle disputes, without a king.

hechos/batalla-de-lechfeld/resumen.texto: Otto I defeated the Hungarians, who stopped raiding Western Europe and settled permanently in the Danube plain.

hechos/oton-i-emperador/resumen.texto: Pope John XII crowned Otto I emperor. The imperial crown became tied to the kings of Germany in what would be called the Holy Roman Empire.

hechos/bautismo-de-polonia/resumen.texto: Duke Mieszko I, married to a Christian princess of Bohemia, was baptized in the Latin rite, which placed Poland in Rome's orbit.

hechos/bautismo-de-la-rus/resumen.texto: Vladimir of Kiev was baptized, married the sister of Emperor Basil II and had the population of Kiev baptized in the Dnieper.

hechos/dinastia-capeta/titulo.texto: Hugh Capet, king of the Franks

hechos/dinastia-capeta/resumen.texto: The great lords of the realm elected Hugh Capet, count of Paris, as king. His dynasty ruled France until 1328, and its branches until 1848.

hechos/reino-de-hungria/titulo.texto: Stephen I crowned king of Hungary

hechos/reino-de-hungria/resumen.texto: Stephen, son of Prince Géza, was crowned with a crown sent by Pope Sylvester II c. 1000 and Christianized the kingdom.

hechos/conversion-de-islandia/resumen.texto: The Althing decided by arbitration that all Icelanders should be baptized, although pagan practice in private was allowed for a time.

hechos/vinland/resumen.texto: Leif Erikson, sailing from Greenland, explored the coast of North America. The Norse settlement of L'Anse aux Meadows, in Newfoundland, confirmed the account of the sagas in 1960.

hechos/fitna-de-al-andalus/resumen.texto: A civil war among Umayyad claimants, Berbers and Slavs destroyed Madinat al-Zahra and ended the caliphate. Al-Andalus split into taifa kingdoms.

hechos/batalla-de-clontarf/resumen.texto: High king Brian Boru defeated the king of Leinster, Máel Mórda, and the Norse kingdom of Dublin, with its allies from Orkney and the Isle of Man, although he died in the battle. The Cogad Gáedel re Gallaib, written a century later for his descendants, told it as the war of the Irish against the foreigners; many historians see it as a war between Irishmen, with Norsemen on both sides.

hechos/cisma-de-oriente/resumen.texto: The papal legates excommunicated Patriarch Michael Cerularius, who responded with an excommunication of his own. Over the centuries the break between the Latin and Greek Churches became permanent.

hechos/conquista-normanda-de-sicilia/res.texto: Roger de Hauteville, brother of Robert Guiscard, conquered Muslim Sicily over thirty years: Palermo fell in 1072. The Normans kept the Arab and Greek administration.

hechos/batalla-de-stamford-bridge/resume.texto: King Harold of England defeated and killed King Harald Hardrada of Norway, who had invaded the north. It is often taken as the end of the Viking Age.

hechos/batalla-de-hastings/resumen.texto: William of Normandy defeated and killed King Harold II. The Norman Conquest changed the nobility, the Church and the language of England.

hechos/querella-de-las-investiduras/resu.texto: Conflict between the papacy and the emperor over the right to appoint bishops, which pitted Gregory VII against Henry IV and ended with the Concordat of Worms.

hechos/canossa/resumen.texto: Henry IV, excommunicated by Gregory VII, waited three days barefoot in the snow before the castle of Canossa until the pope forgave him.

hechos/toma-de-toledo/resumen.texto: The conquest of the old Visigothic capital brought the Christian kingdoms to the Tagus and put the libraries of a learned city in their hands.

hechos/domesday/resumen.texto: William the Conqueror's commissioners traveled across England recording every property: the most complete survey of medieval Europe.

hechos/universidad-de-bolonia-fundacion/.texto: The University of Bologna is born
Irnerius's schools of Roman law in Bologna, which drew students from all over Europe, were traditionally regarded as the first university. Frederick I took its students under his protection in 1158.

hechos/concilio-de-clermont/resumen.texto: Urban II called on the knights of the West to help Byzantium and free Jerusalem, with the promise of the remission of sins. The First Crusade began.

hechos/fundacion-del-cister/resumen.texto: Robert of Molesme and a group of monks founded a monastery at Cîteaux to live the Benedictine Rule more strictly. With Bernard of Clairvaux, the order grew from a few houses to hundreds.

hechos/renacimiento-del-siglo-xii/resume.texto: The schools of Paris, Chartres and Laon, translations from Arabic and Greek, the law of Bologna and Romanesque and Gothic art transformed the culture of Latin Europe.

hechos/concordato-de-worms/resumen.texto: Emperor Henry V and Pope Callixtus II ended the Investiture Controversy by dividing the election of bishops between the Church and the temporal power.

hechos/escuela-de-traductores-de-toledo/.texto: Latin, Jewish and Mozarabic translators rendered into Latin, and later into Castilian, the works of Aristotle, Ptolemy, Galen, Avicenna, Averroes and al-Khwarizmi, which thus reached the universities of Europe.

hechos/condena-de-abelardo/resumen.texto: Accused by Bernard of Clairvaux, Abelard refused to defend himself before the council and appealed to the pope, who confirmed the condemnation of nineteen propositions. He died the following year at Cluny.

hechos/gotico-en-saint-denis/resumen.texto: Abbot Suger rebuilt the choir of his abbey with pointed arches and large stained-glass windows to let light into the church, a theology of light inspired by Pseudo-Dionysius.

hechos/fundacion-de-moscu/resumen.texto: A chronicle records that Prince Yuri Dolgorukiy invited an ally to a banquet in Moscow, then a small fortress in the land of Suzdal.

hechos/conquista-de-lisboa/resumen.texto: Afonso Henriques, first king of Portugal, took Lisbon with the help of English, Flemish and German crusaders on their way to the Holy Land.

hechos/invasion-normanda-de-irlanda/resu.texto: Diarmait Mac Murchada, king of Leinster, driven out in 1166, asked Henry II of England for help and recruited Norman knights from Wales, who landed in 1169; in 1170 Strongbow arrived and married his daughter, and in 1171 Henry II himself, who received the submission of many Irish kings. The Treaty of Windsor (1175) with the high king Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair divided the island. Gerald of Wales told it from the side of the invaders, and Henry invoked the bull Laudabiliter, whose authenticity is debated.

hechos/asesinato-de-becket/resumen.texto: Four of Henry II's knights killed Archbishop Thomas Becket in his cathedral. He was canonized in 1173 and his tomb became the great shrine of England.

hechos/batalla-de-legnano/resumen.texto: The Lombard League of Italian communes defeated Frederick I Barbarossa, who had to recognize their autonomy in the Peace of Constance (1183).

hechos/universidad-de-paris-privilegio/t.texto: Royal privilege granted to the University of Paris

hechos/universidad-de-paris-privilegio/r.texto: Philip II Augustus placed the masters and students of Paris under the jurisdiction of the Church. In 1215 the papal legate gave them statutes, and in 1231 the bull Parens scientiarum confirmed their autonomy.

hechos/saqueo-de-constantinopla/resumen.texto: The Fourth Crusade, diverted by Venice and by a Byzantine pretender, took and sacked Constantinople. The crusaders founded a Latin Empire that lasted until 1261.

hechos/cruzada-albigense/resumen.texto: Innocent III called a crusade against the Cathars of Languedoc. The war, which began with the massacre at Béziers, ended with the south of France subjected to the king.

hechos/orden-franciscana/resumen.texto: Pope Innocent III gave oral approval to the first rule of Francis of Assisi and his companions, who lived by preaching and alms.

hechos/prohibicion-de-aristoteles/titulo.texto: Paris bans the teaching of Aristotle's physics

hechos/prohibicion-de-aristoteles/resume.texto: A synod in Paris banned the public reading of Aristotle's books on natural philosophy and their commentaries. By 1255 they were compulsory in the Faculty of Arts.

hechos/navas-de-tolosa/titulo.texto: Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa

hechos/navas-de-tolosa/resumen.texto: The kings of Castile, Aragon and Navarre defeated the Almohad caliph al-Nasir, which opened the Guadalquivir valley to Christian conquest.

hechos/batalla-de-bouvines/resumen.texto: Philip II Augustus of France defeated Emperor Otto IV and his allies. The defeat of John Lackland led to Magna Carta.

hechos/carta-magna-hecho/resumen.texto: The rebel barons forced King John to seal at Runnymede a charter of liberties that limited royal power.

hechos/iv-concilio-de-letran/resumen.texto: The largest council of the Middle Ages defined transubstantiation, required confession once a year, banned new religious orders and ordered Jews and Muslims to wear distinguishing marks.

hechos/orden-dominica/resumen.texto: Pope Honorius III approved the Order of Preachers of Dominic de Guzmán. The Dominicans soon established themselves at the universities of Paris and Bologna.

hechos/batalla-del-kalka/resumen.texto: A Mongol reconnaissance army defeated the princes of Rus' and their Cuman allies. It was the first clash between the Mongols and Europeans.

hechos/inquisicion-pontificia/resumen.texto: Gregory IX entrusted the Dominicans and Franciscans with special tribunals to prosecute heresy, first in southern France and Germany.

hechos/conquista-de-cordoba/resumen.texto: The former capital of the caliphate passed to Castile, and its great mosque was converted into a cathedral.

hechos/saqueo-de-kiev/resumen.texto: Batu's army took and razed Kiev. Rus' remained subject to the tribute of the Golden Horde for two centuries.

hechos/batalla-de-legnica/resumen.texto: A Mongol army crushed the Poles and the military orders of Duke Henry the Pious, who died in the battle.

hechos/batalla-de-mohi/resumen.texto: Batu's Mongols destroyed the army of King Béla IV of Hungary by the Sajó River and ravaged the kingdom for a year.

hechos/batalla-del-hielo/resumen.texto: Alexander Nevsky, prince of Novgorod, defeated the knights of the Livonian Order on the frozen Lake Peipus.

hechos/conquista-de-sevilla/resumen.texto: After a fifteen-month siege, the Almohad capital of al-Andalus surrendered to Castile. Only the Nasrid kingdom of Granada remained.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-sorbona/resumen.texto: Robert de Sorbon, chaplain to Louis IX, founded a college for poor theology students that gave its name to the university.

hechos/disputa-de-barcelona/resumen.texto: Before James I, Rabbi Nahmanides debated with the Dominican convert Pablo Christiani on whether the Messiah had already come. The king rewarded Nahmanides, but the Dominicans put him on trial.

hechos/condena-de-1270/resumen.texto: Bishop Étienne Tempier condemned thirteen theses of the radical Aristotelians of the Faculty of Arts, among them the unity of the intellect and the eternity of the world.

hechos/ii-concilio-de-lyon/resumen.texto: The council proclaimed a brief union with the Greek Church. Thomas Aquinas died on his way to it, and Bonaventure during its sessions.

hechos/condena-de-1277-hecho/resumen.texto: Tempier condemned 219 philosophical and theological propositions taught in Paris. It was the greatest attempt to set limits on Aristotelian philosophy at the university.

hechos/visperas-sicilianas/resumen.texto: A rebellion that broke out in Palermo on Easter Monday expelled the French of Charles of Anjou. The Sicilians offered the crown to Peter III of Aragon.

hechos/expulsion-judios-inglaterra/titul.texto: Expulsion of the Jews from England

hechos/expulsion-judios-inglaterra/resum.texto: Edward I expelled all Jews from England, the first general expulsion from a European kingdom. They could not legally return until 1656.

hechos/papado-de-avinon/resumen.texto: Seven popes, all French, resided in Avignon, close to the power of the king of France. Gregory XI returned to Rome in 1377.

hechos/juicio-de-los-templarios/resumen.texto: Philip IV had all the Templars in France arrested in 1307 on charges of heresy. The Council of Vienne suppressed the order in 1312, and its grand master was burned in 1314.

hechos/gran-hambruna/resumen.texto: Continuous rains ruined several harvests in northern Europe. Between five and ten percent of the population of many regions died.

hechos/guerra-de-los-cien-anos/resumen.texto: A series of wars between England and France over the inheritance of the French throne and the English possessions on the Continent.

hechos/batalla-de-crecy/resumen.texto: Edward III's English archers destroyed the French cavalry of Philip VI.

hechos/peste-negra/resumen.texto: The plague reached Messina on Genoese ships from Crimea in October 1347 and spread across Europe in four years. Between a third and half of the population died.

hechos/fundacion-universidad-de-praga/ti.texto: Charles IV founds the University of Prague

hechos/fundacion-universidad-de-praga/re.texto: The first university north of the Alps and east of Paris, with four “nations” of students: Bohemians, Bavarians, Poles and Saxons.

hechos/batalla-de-poitiers-1356/resumen.texto: The Black Prince captured King John II of France, who was taken to London.

hechos/bula-de-oro-hecho/resumen.texto: Charles IV established by law that seven prince-electors would elect the King of the Romans without papal intervention.

hechos/dieta-hanseatica/resumen.texto: The merchant cities of the North Sea and the Baltic, led by Lübeck, held their first general assembly. The Hansa dominated the trade of northern Europe until the 15th century.

hechos/jacquerie/resumen.texto: The peasants of the Beauvais region rose up against the nobles after the defeat at Poitiers; the revolt was crushed within a few weeks.

hechos/revuelta-de-los-ciompi/resumen.texto: The wool carders of Florence took over the city's government and created their own guilds, until the merchants regained power in 1382.

hechos/cisma-de-occidente/resumen.texto: After the election of Urban VI, the French cardinals elected another pope in Avignon. Latin Christendom had two and later three popes until the Council of Constance.

hechos/revuelta-de-los-campesinos-1381/r.texto: In protest against a new poll tax, the peasants of Essex and Kent entered London and demanded the end of serfdom. Their leader Wat Tyler died in front of King Richard II.

hechos/union-de-krewo/resumen.texto: Grand Duke Jogaila of Lithuania pledged to be baptized together with his people and to marry Queen Jadwiga of Poland, which united the two states.

hechos/batalla-de-kosovo/resumen.texto: The Serbian army of Prince Lazar faced the Ottomans of Sultan Murad I; both leaders died. Serbia became an Ottoman vassal.

hechos/revueltas-de-1391/resumen.texto: A wave of assaults on the Jewish quarters began in Seville and spread through Castile and Aragon. Thousands of Jews died and many more were forcibly baptized.

hechos/batalla-de-nicopolis/resumen.texto: The Ottomans of Bayezid I destroyed a crusade of French, Burgundians and Hungarians led by Sigismund of Hungary.

hechos/union-de-kalmar/resumen.texto: Queen Margaret I had her grandnephew Eric of Pomerania crowned king of Denmark, Norway and Sweden, which remained united until 1523.

hechos/batalla-de-grunwald/resumen.texto: Poland and Lithuania, under Jogaila and Vytautas, defeated the Teutonic Order in one of the largest battles of medieval Europe.

hechos/disputa-de-tortosa/resumen.texto: Pope Benedict XIII forced the rabbis of Aragon to debate for almost two years with the convert Jerónimo de Santa Fe; many Jews converted.

hechos/concilio-de-constanza/resumen.texto: The council ended the Western Schism by deposing the rival popes and electing Martin V, asserted its authority over the pope and condemned Jan Hus (1415) and Jerome of Prague to the stake.

hechos/batalla-de-azincourt/resumen.texto: Henry V of England and his archers defeated a much larger French army.

hechos/guerras-husitas/resumen.texto: After the Defenestration of Prague in 1419, the Hussites withstood five imperial crusades with Jan Žižka's war wagons. The Compacts of Basel recognized communion with the chalice for the laity.

hechos/sitio-de-orleans/resumen.texto: Joan of Arc entered the city besieged by the English and relieved it in May 1429, which opened the way to the coronation of Charles VII at Reims.

hechos/concilio-de-florencia/resumen.texto: Emperor John VIII, the Patriarch of Constantinople and their theologians agreed to the union of the Churches with Pope Eugene IV, which the Byzantine people rejected. It brought Plethon and Bessarion to Italy.

hechos/batalla-de-varna/resumen.texto: The crusade of King Władysław of Poland and Hungary was destroyed by Sultan Murad II; the king died in the battle.

hechos/imprenta-de-gutenberg/resumen.texto: Gutenberg combined metal type cast in a mold, an oil-based ink and a screw press. By c. 1500 there were printing presses in more than 250 European cities.

hechos/caida-de-constantinopla/resumen.texto: After a siege of almost two months, Mehmed II took Constantinople on 29 May 1453. The last emperor, Constantine XI, died in the fighting.

hechos/batalla-de-castillon/resumen.texto: The French defeated John Talbot's English army with artillery and recovered Gascony. The Hundred Years' War came to an end.

hechos/academia-platonica/resumen.texto: Cosimo de' Medici gave Marsilio Ficino a villa at Careggi to translate Plato; a circle of humanists gathered there around Platonic philosophy.

hechos/gran-parada-del-ugra/titulo.texto: Great Stand on the Ugra River

hechos/gran-parada-del-ugra/resumen.texto: The armies of Ivan III and Khan Akhmat faced each other on the banks of the Ugra without fighting. The Tatar withdrawal marks the end of the Horde's rule over Muscovy.

hechos/novecientas-tesis/resumen.texto: Pico published in Rome 900 theses on philosophy and theology for a public debate. Pope Innocent VIII suspended the debate and condemned thirteen theses.

hechos/toma-de-granada/resumen.texto: After ten years of war, Sultan Boabdil surrendered Granada to the Catholic Monarchs on 2 January 1492. The last Muslim state in the Peninsula came to an end.

hechos/expulsion-judios-espana/titulo.texto: Expulsion of the Jews from Spain

hechos/expulsion-judios-espana/resumen.texto: The Catholic Monarchs ordered the Jews of Castile and Aragon to convert or leave before August. Tens of thousands left for Portugal, Italy, North Africa and the Ottoman Empire.

hechos/primer-viaje-de-colon/resumen.texto: Columbus sailed from Palos on 3 August with three ships, seeking Asia by sailing west, and reached an island in the Bahamas on 12 October.

hechos/batalla-de-fulford/resumen.texto: On 20 September 1066 King Harald Hardrada of Norway, who claimed the English throne, and the exiled Tostig Godwinson defeated the earls Edwin of Mercia and Morcar of Northumbria beside the River Ouse, near York. According to the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle the English initially inflicted many casualties; the figures (about 6,000 Norwegians and 5,000 defenders in combat) are modern estimates. York surrendered in exchange for hostages. Harold II marched from London and defeated the Norwegians five days later at Stamford Bridge; the attrition of the two battles weighed on his confrontation with William at Hastings.

hechos/batalla-de-sluys/resumen.texto: Naval engagement of 24 June 1340, one of the first of the Hundred Years’ War, in the roadstead of Sluis, between Zeeland and Flanders. The English fleet of Edward III (120 to 150 ships) destroyed the French one (about 230 ships), led by Hugues Quiéret and Nicolas Béhuchet, who had tied their ships together in three lines and became entangled. Between 16,000 and 20,000 French deaths are estimated, many by drowning; the figure comes from English, French and Flemish accounts, all partisan. Béhuchet was hanged and Quiéret beheaded.
