It gave England mastery of the Channel, but with little strategic effect: Philip VI rebuilt his fleet and the English siege of Tournai failed.

hechos/concilio-de-lyon-i/resumen.texto: Council that the Catholic Church counts as the 13th ecumenical council, convened by Innocent IV, who had taken refuge in Lyon fleeing Frederick II. With some 250 prelates, almost all from France, Italy and Spain, it met on 28 June and on 5 and 17 July 1245. It deposed and excommunicated the emperor (his envoy, Thaddeus of Suessa, challenged the proceedings as irregular and denied that the council was ecumenical), deposed Sancho II of Portugal, and called the crusade led by Louis IX.

hechos/concilio-de-vienne/resumen.texto: The 15th ecumenical council according to the Catholic Church, convened by Clement V during the Avignon papacy. It met in Vienne, an imperial city at the gates of the kingdom of France, under pressure from Philip IV. Initially undecided about what to do with the Templars, whose arrest in France in 1307 Philip IV had ordered, it gave way when the king arrived in March 1312 and pressed his case: Clement dissolved the order by papal bulls and, by the bull Ad providam (1312), transferred the Templars’ property to the Hospitallers. It condemned the Beghards and Beguines of Germany, set out how to interpret the poverty of the Franciscan rule in the dispute with the Spirituals (constitution Exivi de paradiso), discussed a crusade, and established chairs of Greek, Hebrew, Aramaic and Arabic.

hechos/invasion-mongola-de-europa/resume.texto: A series of Mongol campaigns beginning at Kalka (1223), planned by Subutai and led by Batu and Kadan, grandsons of Genghis Khan. They subdued the Volga Bulgars, the Cumans, the Alans and the Rus’ principalities, and in 1241 invaded Poland (Legnica, 9 April) and Hungary (Mohi, 11 April), as well as raiding the Caucasus, Bulgaria and Croatia. European princes suspended their local wars in the face of the threat and resumed them after the withdrawal of 1242. Scholars debate why the Mongols withdrew: the traditional explanation is the death of the Great Khan Ögedei, while some scholars put more weight on the difficulty of taking stone fortifications without their Chinese and Muslim engineers. Much of Eastern Europe was absorbed into the Golden Horde.

lugares/constantinopla/resumen.texto: The Greek colony of Byzantium, refounded by Constantine in 330 as the new capital of the Roman Empire. It was the largest and richest city of medieval Europe and the Byzantine capital until its conquest by the Ottomans in 1453.

lugares/santa-sofia/resumen.texto: The great church of Constantinople, rebuilt by Justinian between 532 and 537 with a dome unrivaled in its time. It was the seat of the patriarch until 1453, when Mehmed II converted it into a mosque.

lugares/ravena/resumen.texto: Capital of the Western Empire from 402, of the kingdoms of Odoacer and Theodoric, and later of the Byzantine exarchate until 751. Its 5th- and 6th-century mosaics are the largest ensemble of Early Christian and Byzantine art in the West.

lugares/pavia/resumen.texto: The ancient Ticinum, capital of the Lombard kingdom from 572 and later of the Kingdom of Italy. Boethius was imprisoned and died there, and its school of law trained Lanfranc.

lugares/milan/resumen.texto: Imperial capital in the 4th century and seat of Bishop Ambrose, who baptized Augustine in 387. From the 12th century it was one of the great communes of Lombardy and, under the Visconti and the Sforza, the capital of a duchy.

lugares/venecia/resumen.texto: Maritime republic that arose on the islands of the lagoon, governed by a doge from the late 7th century. It dominated trade with the East, diverted the Fourth Crusade toward Constantinople and was the great center of printing in the late 15th century.

lugares/genova/resumen.texto: Maritime republic, rival of Venice and Pisa, with colonies on the Black Sea and the Aegean. Marco Polo dictated his book of travels in its prisons.

lugares/pisa/resumen.texto: Maritime republic of the 11th to 13th centuries, with trade throughout the Mediterranean. Leonardo Fibonacci was born and worked there; he learned Arabic arithmetic in the Pisan port of Bugia.

lugares/florencia/resumen.texto: Tuscan commune enriched by banking and wool. It was the city of Dante, Petrarch and Boccaccio and, under the Medici, the cradle of humanism and of the revival of Platonism.

lugares/napoles/resumen.texto: A Greek city, later a Byzantine duchy and from 1266 the capital of the Angevin and Aragonese kingdom of southern Italy. Frederick II founded a university there in 1224 to train his officials.

lugares/salerno/resumen.texto: Roman colony and capital of a Lombard principality. Its school of medicine, the oldest in Europe, brought together Greek, Latin, Arabic and Jewish medicine from the 10th century.

lugares/amalfi/resumen.texto: The first of the Italian maritime republics, active in trade with Byzantium and Egypt from the 9th to the 11th century.

lugares/asis/resumen.texto: Umbrian city where Francis of Assisi and Clare were born, and site of the Basilica of San Francesco, decorated by Giotto and Cimabue.

lugares/montecassino/resumen.texto: Monastery founded by Benedict of Nursia c. 529, cradle of the Benedictine order. In the 11th century, under Abbot Desiderius and Constantine the African, it was a center for copying manuscripts and translating Arabic medicine.

lugares/bobbio/resumen.texto: Monastery founded by the Irishman Columbanus in 614. Its library gathered manuscripts of classical texts, some preserved only in palimpsests.

lugares/palermo/resumen.texto: Founded by the Phoenicians, it was the capital of the Emirate of Sicily from 831 and later of the Norman kingdom, where Latin, Greek and Arabic culture coexisted. Al-Idrisi worked there and Frederick II ruled from it.

lugares/paris/resumen.texto: The Lutetia of the Parisii, which Caesar places on an island in the Seine (VII.57); where the Gaulish settlement was is debated since, at Nanterre, an agglomeration of 15 hectares from that period appeared. It was the capital of the Capetians from the late 10th century and, in the 12th and 13th centuries, the great intellectual center of Europe: its schools of Notre-Dame, St Victor and St Genevieve gave rise to the university.

lugares/universidad-de-paris/resumen.texto: It arose from the association of the masters and students of the Parisian schools and received privileges from the king in 1200 and statutes in 1215. Its faculty of theology, with Albertus Magnus, Thomas Aquinas, Bonaventure and Duns Scotus, was the most prestigious in Christendom.

lugares/saint-denis/resumen.texto: Royal abbey near Paris, burial place of the kings of France. Abbot Suger's rebuilding between 1137 and 1144 inaugurated Gothic architecture.

lugares/chartres/resumen.texto: Its cathedral school, with Fulbert, Bernard, Thierry and William of Conches, was the center of Platonism and of the study of the liberal arts in the 11th and 12th centuries. Its Gothic cathedral was rebuilt after the fire of 1194.

lugares/reims/resumen.texto: City where the kings of France were consecrated since the baptism of Clovis. Its cathedral school was famous under Gerbert of Aurillac in the late 10th century.

lugares/laon/resumen.texto: Carolingian city on a hill in Picardy. Its school, under Anselm of Laon in the early 12th century, was the great school of theology before the rise of Paris; manuscripts of the 9th-century Irish masters are preserved there.

lugares/tours/resumen.texto: City of the tomb of Saint Martin, the great shrine of Gaul. Its bishop Gregory wrote the History of the Franks, and Alcuin died as abbot of Saint-Martin.

lugares/orleans/resumen.texto: City on the Loire with a school of classical authors and later of law. Its relief by Joan of Arc in 1429 changed the course of the Hundred Years' War.

lugares/lyon/resumen.texto: The ancient Lugdunum, a colony founded in 43 BC by Lucius Munatius Plancus with a Gaulish name, Lugudunon; it was capital of Gallia Lugdunensis and seat of the altar of the Three Gauls. Two ecumenical councils were held there, in 1245 and 1274, and it was a great center of fairs and printing at the end of the 15th century.

lugares/avinon/resumen.texto: City in Provence where the popes resided between 1309 and 1377, as did the popes of the Avignon obedience during the Western Schism. The papal court attracted jurists, bankers and humanists such as Petrarch.

lugares/toulouse/resumen.texto: Capital of the Visigothic kingdom until 507 and later of the County of Toulouse, a center of Occitan culture and of the troubadours. It was the scene of the crusade against the Cathars and of the founding of the Dominicans.

lugares/montpellier/resumen.texto: City founded in the 10th century, a lordship of the kings of Aragon and Majorca. Its school of medicine, with statutes from 1220, rivaled that of Salerno.

lugares/troyes/resumen.texto: City of the Champagne fairs, the great market of Europe in the 12th and 13th centuries. Chrétien de Troyes wrote his romances of Arthur's court there.

lugares/poitiers/resumen.texto: Capital of the County of Poitou and the Duchy of Aquitaine, court of William IX and Eleanor of Aquitaine.

lugares/ruan/resumen.texto: Capital of the Duchy of Normandy from 911. Joan of Arc was tried and burned there in 1431.

lugares/cluny/resumen.texto: Benedictine abbey founded in 910, head of a network of hundreds of monasteries exempt from the authority of bishops and laymen. It drove the reform of the Church, and its third church was the largest in Christendom until the 16th century.

lugares/cister/resumen.texto: Burgundian abbey founded in 1098 by Robert of Molesme, origin of the Cistercian order, which sought to return to the poverty and work of the Benedictine Rule.

lugares/claraval/resumen.texto: Cistercian abbey founded by Bernard in 1115, from which dozens of monasteries were founded throughout Europe.

lugares/bec/resumen.texto: Norman abbey where Lanfranc and Anselm taught, the most famous monastic school of the 11th century.

lugares/fulda/resumen.texto: Monastery founded by a disciple of Boniface, missionary to Germania. Under Rabanus Maurus it was a great Carolingian center of learning.

lugares/reichenau/resumen.texto: Monastery on an island in Lake Constance, a center of manuscript copying and illumination from the 9th to the 11th century.

lugares/st-gallen/resumen.texto: Swiss abbey founded on the hermitage of the Irishman Gall. Its library holds one of the largest collections of early medieval manuscripts and the Plan of Saint Gall, an ideal 9th-century monastery.

lugares/aquisgran/resumen.texto: Spa town where Charlemagne built his palace and Palatine Chapel, center of the Carolingian court and palace school. The kings of Germany were crowned there until 1531.

lugares/colonia/resumen.texto: Roman colony and later a great archbishopric and commercial city on the Rhine. Albertus Magnus, Thomas Aquinas and Duns Scotus taught there, and its university was founded in 1388.

lugares/maguncia/resumen.texto: Seat of the primate archbishop of Germany and prince-elector. Gutenberg perfected movable-type printing there and printed his Bible.

lugares/treveris/resumen.texto: One of the capitals of the late Roman Empire and later an electoral archbishopric. Nicholas of Cusa was born nearby, in Kues, and left his library there.

lugares/magdeburgo/resumen.texto: Favorite city of Otto I and an archbishopric from 968 for the mission among the Slavs. Its town law was copied in hundreds of cities in Central Europe.

lugares/lubeck/resumen.texto: Baltic city refounded in 1159 by Henry the Lion, head of the Hanseatic League.

lugares/viena/resumen.texto: The ancient Vindobona, capital of the Babenbergs from 1155 and later of the Habsburgs. Its university was founded in 1365.

lugares/brujas/resumen.texto: Great port of the County of Flanders, market for English wool and Flemish cloth, with offices of the Hansa and of Italian bankers.

lugares/gante/resumen.texto: Cloth-making city of Flanders, one of the most populous in northern Europe in the 14th century.

lugares/hedeby/resumen.texto: The largest trading town of the Danes in the Viking Age, in southern Jutland. It was destroyed in 1066 and replaced by Schleswig.

lugares/birka/resumen.texto: Viking trading center on an island in Lake Mälaren, in Sweden, where the missionary Ansgar preached c. 830.

lugares/gamla-uppsala/resumen.texto: Center of the Swedish kings, with great burial mounds from the 5th and 6th centuries. Adam of Bremen describes its pagan temple c. 1075; in the 12th century it became the seat of the archbishop of Sweden.

lugares/nidaros/resumen.texto: City founded by King Olaf Tryggvason, with the tomb of Saint Olaf, the great shrine of Scandinavia, and seat of the archbishop of Norway from 1152.

lugares/bergen/resumen.texto: Capital of Norway in the 13th century and port of the dried-cod trade, with a Hansa office.

lugares/lund/resumen.texto: City in Scania, then Danish, seat from 1104 of the archbishop of all Scandinavia.

lugares/thingvellir/resumen.texto: Plain in southwestern Iceland where the Althing, the assembly of all the free men of the island, met from 930. Christianity was accepted there in the year 1000.

lugares/skalholt/resumen.texto: Seat of the first bishop of Iceland from 1056 and center of the island's written culture.

lugares/londres/resumen.texto: Roman Londinium, abandoned and later refounded by the Anglo-Saxons, was the principal city and port of England and the seat of royal government at Westminster.

lugares/winchester/resumen.texto: Capital of the kingdom of Wessex and of Alfred the Great, where the royal treasury and the Domesday Book were kept.

lugares/canterbury/resumen.texto: Seat of the primate archbishop of England since Augustine's mission in 597. Lanfranc and Anselm were archbishops there, and Thomas Becket was murdered there in 1170.

lugares/york/resumen.texto: Roman Eboracum, seat of an archbishopric and capital of the Viking kings of Jórvík. Its cathedral school trained Alcuin.

lugares/universidad-de-oxford/resumen.texto: Teaching took place in Oxford from the late 11th century, and the university grew from 1167, when the king forbade the English to study in Paris. With Grosseteste, Roger Bacon, Duns Scotus, Ockham and the Merton Calculators, it was the great center of logic and natural philosophy.

lugares/universidad-de-cambridge/resumen.texto: Founded by masters who left Oxford in 1209 after a clash with the town.

lugares/lindisfarne/resumen.texto: Monastery on an island in Northumbria founded by the Irishman Aidan. The Lindisfarne Gospels were illuminated there, and in 793 it suffered the first great Viking raid.

lugares/jarrow/resumen.texto: Twin monastery in Northumbria with an exceptional library brought from Rome, where Bede the Venerable lived and wrote.

lugares/sutton-hoo/resumen.texto: Burial ground of the kings of East Anglia. The ship burial excavated in 1939, from c. 625, is the greatest find of Anglo-Saxon England.

lugares/iona/resumen.texto: Monastery founded by the Irishman Columba around 563 on an island off Scotland, from which the mission to Northumbria (Lindisfarne, 635) and, according to Bede, the mission to the Picts set out. After the Viking attacks of 795 to 806 the community founded Kells; the Book of Kells was probably begun on Iona.

lugares/armagh/resumen.texto: Church associated with St Patrick and seat of the primate of Ireland. Its foundation by Patrick and its primacy rest on texts produced by Armagh itself from the 7th century, such as the Life by Muirchú and the Liber Angeli, copied into the Book of Armagh around 807; Patrick's own writings do not name it.

lugares/clonmacnoise/resumen.texto: Great Irish monastery on the River Shannon, founded by Ciarán. It was a center of learning and chronicles, such as the Annals of Tigernach. There, around 1100, the Lebor na hUidre was copied, the oldest surviving manuscript written in Irish.

lugares/kells/resumen.texto: Monastery founded by monks from Iona fleeing the Vikings. It gave its name to the Book of Kells, which was kept there for centuries.

lugares/dublin/resumen.texto: Founded as a Viking base in 841, it was the main Norse kingdom of Ireland until the arrival of the Anglo-Normans in 1170.

lugares/toledo/resumen.texto: The Toletum of the Carpetani, which Marcus Fulvius Nobilior took around 193-192 BC (Livy XXXV), and capital of the Visigothic kingdom and seat of its councils. Conquered by Alfonso VI in 1085, it was the great bridge between Arabic science and Latin Europe thanks to its translators.

lugares/cordoba/resumen.texto: Capital of the Umayyad emirate and caliphate of al-Andalus, the largest city in Western Europe in the 10th century, with the library of al-Hakam II. Ibn Hazm, Averroes and Maimonides were born there.

lugares/mezquita-de-cordoba/resumen.texto: Great mosque of the Umayyads, begun by Abd al-Rahman I in 785 and enlarged until the 10th century. It has been a cathedral since 1236.

lugares/medina-azahara/resumen.texto: Palatine city built by Abd al-Rahman III near Córdoba as the seat of the caliphate. It was sacked and abandoned in the civil war that followed 1009.

lugares/sevilla/resumen.texto: The Roman Hispalis, see of Bishop Isidore in the Visigothic period, capital of the Almohads in al-Andalus and, from 1248, a city of the kings of Castile.

lugares/granada/resumen.texto: Capital of a Zirid taifa kingdom and, from 1238, of the Nasrid kingdom, the last Muslim state on the Peninsula, with its palace of the Alhambra. It was taken by the Catholic Monarchs in 1492.

lugares/zaragoza/resumen.texto: The Iberian Salduie, whose inhabitants won in 87 BC the lawsuit recorded in the Tabula Contrebiensis; then Roman Caesaraugusta, capital of a cultured taifa in the 11th century, where Ibn Gabirol and Avempace lived, and from 1118 capital of the kingdom of Aragon.

lugares/barcelona/resumen.texto: Capital of the County of Barcelona and great port of the Crown of Aragon. The 1263 disputation between Nachmanides and Pablo Christiani was held there.

lugares/lisboa/resumen.texto: The Olisipo that Decimus Junius Brutus fortified in 138 BC (Strabo III.3.1); a Muslim city taken in 1147 by Afonso Henriques with the help of crusaders, and capital of Portugal from the 13th century.

lugares/oviedo/resumen.texto: Capital of the kingdom of Asturias from the late 8th century, the core of the Christian kingdoms of the north.

lugares/leon/resumen.texto: Former camp of the Legio VII, capital of the kingdom of León from 910.

lugares/santiago-de-compostela/resumen.texto: City that grew up around the tomb attributed to the apostle James, discovered c. 820-830. The Way of St James made it one of the three great pilgrimage destinations of Christendom.

lugares/burgos/resumen.texto: City founded in 884, head of Castile and frequent residence of its kings.

lugares/ripoll/resumen.texto: Monastery in Catalonia with a library where, in the 10th century, scientific texts translated from Arabic were copied and studied by Gerbert of Aurillac.

lugares/san-millan/resumen.texto: Monastery in La Rioja where the Glosas Emilianenses were written c. 1000, among the first texts in Castilian Romance and in Basque.

lugares/universidad-de-bolonia/resumen.texto: The oldest university in Europe, born from the schools of Roman and canon law of Irnerius and Gratian. It was the model for student universities.

lugares/universidad-de-salamanca/resumen.texto: Founded by Alfonso IX of León in 1218, the oldest of the Spanish universities still in operation.

lugares/universidad-de-padua/resumen.texto: Founded by masters and students who left Bologna in 1222. It was a great center of medicine and Aristotelian philosophy.

lugares/universidad-de-napoles/resumen.texto: The first university founded by a sovereign, Frederick II, in 1224. Thomas Aquinas studied there.

lugares/universidad-de-montpellier/resum.texto: Its faculty of medicine received statutes in 1220, and the pope recognized the university in 1289.

lugares/universidad-de-toulouse/resumen.texto: Founded in 1229 as part of the peace that ended the Albigensian Crusade, to combat heresy with theologians.

lugares/universidad-de-praga/resumen.texto: The first university in Central Europe, founded by Charles IV in 1348. Jan Hus was its rector.

lugares/universidad-de-cracovia/resumen.texto: Founded by Casimir III in 1364 and refounded by Jogaila in 1400. Copernicus studied there.

lugares/universidad-de-viena/resumen.texto: Founded by Duke Rudolf IV in 1365.

lugares/universidad-de-heidelberg/resume.texto: The oldest university in present-day Germany, founded by the Elector Palatine in 1386.

lugares/universidad-de-colonia/resumen.texto: Founded by the city in 1388, building on the tradition of the Dominican studies of Albertus Magnus.

lugares/universidad-de-lovaina/resumen.texto: Founded in 1425 in the Duchy of Brabant, it was a great center of humanism in the 16th century.

lugares/universidad-de-st-andrews/resume.texto: The oldest university in Scotland, recognized by the pope in 1413.

lugares/universidad-de-upsala/resumen.texto: The first university in Scandinavia, founded in 1477.

lugares/gniezno/resumen.texto: First center of the Piasts and seat of the archbishopric of Poland from the year 1000, when Emperor Otto III visited it.

lugares/cracovia/resumen.texto: Capital of the kingdom of Poland from the 11th century until 1596, with Wawel Castle and the coronation cathedral.

lugares/marienburg/resumen.texto: The largest brick castle in Europe, seat of the Grand Master of the Teutonic Order between 1309 and 1457.

lugares/praga/resumen.texto: Capital of the Přemyslids and of the kings of Bohemia. Under Charles IV it was the capital of the Holy Roman Empire, and in the 15th century the center of the Hussite movement.

lugares/esztergom/resumen.texto: Seat of Prince Géza and his son Stephen I, first king of Hungary, crowned there c. 1000; seat of the primate archbishop.

lugares/buda/resumen.texto: Castle and town founded after the Mongol invasion, capital of the kingdom of Hungary from the 14th century. Matthias Corvinus assembled there one of the largest libraries of his time.

lugares/pannonhalma/resumen.texto: Benedictine abbey founded in 996, one of the first Christian centers of Hungary.

lugares/preslav/resumen.texto: Capital of the First Bulgarian Empire from 893, center of the literary school that spread the Cyrillic script.

lugares/ohrid/resumen.texto: City on Lake Ohrid where Clement founded a school of Slavic letters in 886. It was the seat of an autocephalous archbishopric.

lugares/tarnovo/resumen.texto: Capital of the Second Bulgarian Empire from 1185 until the Ottoman conquest of 1393.

lugares/ragusa/resumen.texto: Maritime republic on the Adriatic, free from 1358 under Hungarian and later Ottoman protection, an intermediary in the trade of the Balkans.

lugares/tesalonica/resumen.texto: Second city of the Byzantine Empire. Cyril and Methodius came from there, and their local Slavic became a written language; Gregory Palamas was archbishop there.

lugares/monte-athos/resumen.texto: Peninsula of Orthodox monasteries since the founding of the Great Lavra in 963. It was the center of Hesychasm in the 14th century.

lugares/mistra/resumen.texto: Fortress built by the crusaders in 1249 and Byzantine capital of the Despotate of the Morea, where Gemistos Plethon taught.

lugares/kiev/resumen.texto: Capital of Kievan Rus' from the late 9th century. Its people were baptized there in 988, the Chronicle of Nestor was written there and St Sophia's Cathedral was built; the Mongols sacked it in 1240.

lugares/novgorod/resumen.texto: Trading city of northern Rus', a republic governed by its assembly (veche) until 1478. Its birch-bark letters show everyday medieval writing.

lugares/vladimir/resumen.texto: Capital of the principality of Vladimir-Suzdal in the 12th and 13th centuries, heir to the prestige of Kyiv.

lugares/moscu/resumen.texto: First mentioned in 1147, it grew as the capital of the principality of Muscovy, which unified the Russian lands and freed itself from Mongol rule in 1480.

lugares/vilna/resumen.texto: Capital of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, first mentioned in the letters of Grand Duke Gediminas in 1323.

lugares/riga/resumen.texto: City founded in 1201 by Bishop Albert, base of the Livonian Crusade and member of the Hanseatic League.

lugares/biblioteca-marciana/resumen.texto: Library in Venice born from Cardinal Bessarion's donation of Greek and Latin manuscripts in 1468.

lugares/biblioteca-vaticana/resumen.texto: Formally founded by Pope Sixtus IV in 1475 on the collection assembled by Nicholas V.
